title: Reproduction vs. replication: same vs. different data
guidance: In this handbook, a reproduction re-analyses the same data, while a replication analyses different data. Different data can even be a distinct, non-overlapping subset of the same sample (e.g., panel data). Because fields use these terms inconsistently (some reverse them), define your terms explicitly in your write-up.
action: State explicitly in your report whether your study is a reproduction or a replication, and define both terms.
quote: replication is used to refer to efforts involving the analysis of different data, and reproduction to efforts involving the same data

title: 'Replicated' describes an attempt, 'replicable' an outcome
guidance: Everyday language conflates the study with its outcome: 'has been replicated' often means 'was corroborated'. The handbook uses 'was replicated' for any attempt regardless of result, and 'replicable' only when the original hypothesis was supported. Whether an outcome counts as success depends on the success criteria applied.
action: Use consistent wording that separates the replication attempt from its outcome throughout your manuscript.
quote: when we state that a “study was reproduced/replicated” we mean that there has been a replication attempt, irrespective of its outcome

title: Closeness can only be judged against theory
guidance: Replication types are defined by how similar the new study is to the original, but similarity cannot be judged without a theory of the concepts involved. From a deductive view, only changes that affect the underlying theory matter; e.g., a change of season matters for a study on tea preferences but not for color perception.
action: For each difference from the original, note whether theory suggests it is relevant to the effect.
quote: Similarity cannot be evaluated without a theory about the concepts involved

title: Procedural fidelity may undermine theoretical equivalence
guidance: Contextually sensitive topics (dependent on time, culture, or population) replicated less often even with high methodological fidelity. Reusing outdated stimuli (e.g., old celebrities) may be psychologically inert, so strict copying can make a replication less valid. Consider whether adapting stimuli better preserves the intended psychological process.
action: Judge whether your original stimuli still carry the same meaning in your population and time.
quote: strict methodological similarity might paradoxically undermine theoretical closeness, and thus the validity of the replication attempt

title: Close replications test credibility; conceptual ones test generalizability
guidance: Since deviations from the original have mostly uncertain consequences, close replications most directly test whether original results are credible. Conceptual replications that vary design features instead address generalizability. Seemingly irrelevant design choices (e.g., text vs. image stimuli) have produced opposite conclusions in past work.
action: Decide and state whether your primary aim is testing credibility (close) or generalizability (conceptual).
quote: close replications more directly test the credibility of original results, while conceptual replications that vary features of the design are concerned with

title: Check that your replication speaks to the original claim
guidance: A replication should be a study whose any outcome is diagnostic for the prior claim. Testing a claim outside its stated scope (e.g., moving from maths to science education) may need to be framed differently. If the original authors did not specify scope, you may treat the claim as broad, so generalization attempts are relevant.
action: Write down the original claim and its stated scope, and confirm your design falls within it.
quote: This can lead to issues when the original claim is not clear on its boundary conditions

title: Menu of repetitive-research types
guidance: Types range from computational and recoding reproductions (correctness of the report), robustness reproductions and multiverse analyses (robustness), to close replications, close replications with extension, and conceptual/constructive replications (generalizability, theory validity). Choosing among them is the first step in planning.
action: Select one type from the handbook's Table 4.1 and record its goal in your plan.
quote: The decision between these types is the first step in planning

title: Replications suit student research teams
guidance: Replications can take substantial resources, so team formation matters. Repetitive research has been successfully run collaboratively with graduate and undergraduate students, and the authors recommend using replications to involve students of all levels in conducting and publishing research.
action: Form a replication team and assign roles early, considering involving students at different levels.
quote: we recommend the use of replication studies to engage students of different levels in conducting and publishing research

title: Justify and transparently report target selection
guidance: There is no single correct way to choose what to replicate; it depends on goals (e.g., building on a finding vs. doubting it) and practical constraints. What matters is that the choice is well justified and openly communicated. A structured replication target selection checklist (Pittelkow et al., 2023) can help.
action: Write a transparent justification for your target study, e.g., using the Pittelkow et al. (2023) checklist.
quote: what does matter is that the selection of reproduction and replication targets is well justified and transparently communicated

title: Evidence the value of the original study
guidance: Value can be shown by the study having started a research stream, citations, theoretical relevance, and implications for practice, policy or clinical work; societal impact also counts. Note that citations may be negative. If you want to build on the finding in your own programme, that interest can itself indicate relevance.
action: Document citation impact, theoretical relevance, and practical/societal implications of your target study.
quote: the theoretical relevance of the study, and the implications of the original study for practice, policy, or clinical work

title: Higher uncertainty means more to learn
guidance: The more uncertain the original finding, the more a replication can teach. Evidence strength varies: Registered Reports are typically more convincing than non-preregistered studies, and sample size has been proposed as an indicator. Meta-analytic checks help but none beats a well-designed replication.
action: Assess the original evidence strength (preregistration, sample size, prior replications) as part of your justification.
quote: The more uncertain the original study’s outcome is, the higher the potential of knowledge gained from reproduction and replication

title: Too many significant studies is a warning sign
guidance: With several studies each at modest power, all being significant is unlikely even if the hypothesis is true (ten studies at 90% power: about .35; five at 80%: about .33). Multi-study papers reporting only significant results with non-very-high power should be treated with caution.
action: Count significant vs. non-significant studies in the original paper and consider its implied power.
quote: studies reporting a set of many and only significant findings when each of the studies does not have very high power should be taken with caution

title: Replicate the original inside any extension
guidance: If you suspect an effect depends on context or a moderator, include a replication of the original condition within the new study for the argument to work. This also guards against later claims of 'hidden moderators'.
action: When testing a moderator or new context, include a condition that replicates the original finding.
quote: the original finding needs to be replicated in a part of the new study for the argument to work

title: Handle vague theories with author input
guidance: Vague theories invite claims that a failed replication misunderstood the theory. Rather than avoiding such targets, ask original authors for feedback on your protocol before data collection, or run an adversarial collaboration ('red teaming') to agree on a diagnostic design.
action: Send your draft protocol to the original authors for feedback before collecting data.
quote: replication researchers can ask original authors for feedback on the study protocol before collecting data

title: Search for existing reproductions and replications
guidance: The first reproduction or replication reduces uncertainty the most, so check what already exists. Useful resources include the Institute for Replication discussion papers, ReplicationWiki, the CODECHECK register, the Social Science Reproduction Platform, and the FORRT Replication Database, supplemented by manual searches.
action: Search FReD, ReplicationWiki, I4R, CODECHECK and SSRP plus a manual search for prior repetitions.
quote: the search for existing reproductions and replications is a key part of the selection of a target study

title: Replicators are biased too
guidance: Original authors may have confirmation bias, motivated reasoning or financial conflicts, but replicators are equally prone to bias: interest in failed replications may tempt 'null hacking', and personal admiration or envy may drive target choice. Preregistration and Registered Reports largely address p-hacking and null-hacking.
action: Reflect on and disclose your own motivations and conflicts of interest regarding the target.
quote: replication researchers are just as prone to bias as original authors can be

title: Match the target to your resources
guidance: Replications often need several times the original sample size, and some designs (longitudinal studies, MRI) need special equipment and expertise. Anticipate practical problems and pick a target your funding, time, equipment and expertise can support, to avoid research waste.
action: Estimate required sample size, cost, time and expertise, and confirm your team can deliver.
quote: should restrict their choice of replication target to align with their lab resources in order to prevent ‘secondary’ research waste

title: Search post-publication discussions
guidance: Comments, critiques, error reports, reinterpretations and replication suggestions about the target may change how you should design your study. Look for published comments, reviews, blog posts and social media discussion via Altmetric, PubPeer, or Hypothes.is.
action: Search Altmetric and PubPeer for commentary on your target study and note design implications.
quote: replication researchers should look for post-publication discussions on the target study such as published comments and reviews, blog posts, or discussions on social media

title: Reproduce before you replicate
guidance: Many features of a replication rest on the original report being correct. A reproduction can reveal coding errors, fraud, and sensitivity to analytic decisions, and can take minutes to weeks. To use resources well, check reproducibility and robustness before planning a replication.
action: Attempt a reproduction of the original analysis before finalising your replication design.
quote: we encourage researchers to investigate the original finding’s reproducibility and robustness first

title: Software versions and missing seeds cause discrepancies
guidance: Even with original code and data, different software versions or defaults can produce small deviations, and without a set random seed, analyses like bootstrapping cannot be reproduced exactly. Anticipate and document such differences rather than treating them as errors.
action: Record software versions and note any analyses depending on random numbers without a seed.
quote: differences in software versions or default settings may lead to slight deviations or require corrections in some cases

title: Recoding reproduction when no script exists
guidance: Without original code, rebuild the analysis from the report. Pay special attention to outlier exclusion, variable transformations and missing-data handling, which are often incompletely described, especially in older research.
action: List every processing step (exclusions, transformations, missing data) from the paper before recoding.
quote: special attention should be paid to processing steps such as exclusion of outliers, transformation of variables, and handling of missing data

title: Run small robustness alterations
guidance: Test the finding's robustness with small changes to processing and analysis, e.g., a different age range or a ±2 instead of ±3 SD outlier cut-off. Start with choices not determined by theory. If the original was preregistered, check whether its analyses followed the plan.
action: Vary at least one theory-irrelevant analytic choice (e.g., outlier rule) and report the effect.
quote: we recommend testing the robustness of the original finding by making small alterations to the data processing and analyses procedure

title: Check reported statistics without data
guidance: If neither code nor data are available, no reproduction is possible, but you can still check whether reported p-values match their test statistics using statcheck.io, the statcheck R package, or papercheck.
action: Run statcheck on the original paper if its data and code are unavailable.
quote: If neither code nor data are available (or shared by the authors), no reproduction is possible

title: Close replication before conceptual replication
guidance: To build generalizability, start with replications as close as possible to the original, and only later move to conceptual ones. From constructive replications onward, try to improve the original (more valid measures, better controls, more representative samples) and avoid 'quasi-random' changes lacking clear rationale.
action: Justify each intended variation with a clear rationale; avoid unmotivated changes.
quote: we also suggest starting with replications that adhere as close as possible to the original study

title: Locate data and code for reproductions
guidance: Data and code are often linked in the paper or deposited in repositories (Zenodo, OSF, GitHub, GitLab) or supplements. To find reproducible targets, topfactor.org (data transparency level 3) and Kranz's economics database can help.
action: Search the paper, supplements and repositories (OSF, Zenodo, GitHub) for data and code.
quote: These are usually linked within the manuscript and shared via repositories (e.g., Zenodo, OSF.io, github.com, gitlab.com)

title: Contacting original authors effectively
guidance: Expect to contact authors more than once, as missing details surface during planning. Verify the corresponding author's current email by web search, consider writing to the last author or copying all authors, and use the handbook's email templates (Appendix E). Some authors may not respond.
action: Verify current author emails and send a materials request using an Appendix E template.
quote: We recommend a quick web search to check if this is the current email address, as researchers frequently change institutions

title: Identify and justify the claim you reproduce
guidance: Analyses always serve to evaluate a claim. Focus typically on results essential to the paper's main argument, though secondary results can be justified if relevant elsewhere. Either way, justify your choice of claim in the report.
action: Name the specific claim you reproduce and justify why it was chosen.
quote: reproduction researchers need to justify the choice of the claim in their report

title: Preregister reproductions beyond numerical checks
guidance: Preregistration limits researcher degrees of freedom and can prevent null hacking or 'gotcha bias', provided the whole analysis plan is registered before accessing data. A numerical reproduction with available code needs no preregistration, but specify all further analyses in advance.
action: Preregister all robustness and additional analyses before accessing the original data.
quote: While a numerical reproduction with available code does not require preregistration, we recommend a priori specification of all further planned analyses

title: Document your computing environment
guidance: Reproduction success can depend on the machine's software, program versions, and packages. In R, include sessionInfo() output in supplementary materials; Python users can use session_info.show().
action: Include sessionInfo() (R) or session_info.show() (Python) output in your supplements.
quote: using the function sessionInfo(), which should be included in supplementary materials

title: Report reproducibility indicators and dashboards
guidance: Structure the report so numerical reproduction, alternative analyses, and exploratory analyses are clearly separated. Include reproducibility indicators summarising significance and relative effect sizes across original and reproduction, ideally visualised with a reproducibility dashboard and specification curves.
action: Report reproducibility indicators comparing significance and effect sizes, with a specification curve.
quote: the reproduction report should include reproducibility indicators (Dreber & Johannesson, 2024) that summarize statistical significance and relative effect sizes

title: Preregister analysis plan and success criteria
guidance: Because replications meet skepticism, preregister the replication including the analysis plan (ideally code tested on simulated or pilot data) and criteria distinguishing success from failure. A preregistration without an analysis plan does not guard against p-hacking. Criteria can be sequential, e.g., requiring a working manipulation check.
action: Preregister tested analysis code and explicit criteria for replication success and failure.
quote: A preregistration without an analysis plan provides no safeguard against p-hacking

title: Templates and Registered Report routes
guidance: Brandt et al. (2014) offer a replication preregistration template, though it may not suit designs outside social psychology; OSF lists other templates. Consider a Registered Report, where rejection based on results is not possible, or Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI-RR), whose acceptance can lead to publication in PCI-friendly journals.
action: Choose a preregistration template and consider submitting as a Registered Report or via PCI-RR.
quote: A rejection due to the results is not possible at this point. A list of journals offering Registered Reports

title: Handle deviations from the preregistration openly
guidance: Deviating from your plan is not wrong in itself, but list and discuss all changes and show how they affected the results. If you notice changes during data collection, upload amendments with version history on your registration platform.
action: Log each deviation from your preregistration and report its impact on results.
quote: all changes should be listed, discussed, and it should be made transparent how the changes affected the results

title: Don't reuse the original sample size
guidance: Although you should stay close to the original otherwise, replication samples usually need to be larger: an informative failure must provide evidence for a null or a substantially smaller effect. See Lakens (2022) for general sample size justification.
action: Justify a sample size larger than the original rather than copying it.
quote: we advise against simply using the original study’s sample size

title: Multiple effect sizes reduce total power
guidance: If success requires all of several effects (scales, items, groups, hypotheses) to be significant, total power is lower than each test's power. With limited resources, designate one central effect size or specify how results will be aggregated (e.g., multivariate models).
action: Designate a single focal effect or specify an aggregation method before computing power.
quote: If the interpretation will rely on the significance of all effect sizes, the total power will be smaller than the power for each individual test

title: Small telescopes approach
guidance: Test whether the replication effect is smaller than the effect the original study had 33% power to detect; if so, the original can be treated as uninformative. This suits imprecise originals with wide confidence intervals. It needs 2.5 times the original N for 80% power, but the handbook recommends 95% power, requiring about 4.5 times the original N.
action: Compute the d33% effect and plan N at about 4.5 times the original for 95% power.
quote: This requires a multiple of 4.5 (rather than 2.5, see Wallrich, 2025)

title: Equivalence testing with a SESOI
guidance: If you can justify a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), plan to test whether the replication effect is significantly smaller than it using a one-sided test in the 'lesser' direction, since the original fixes the direction. Lakens et al. (2018) provide a tutorial.
action: Define and justify a SESOI and plan a one-sided test against it.
quote: If statements can be made about the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), researchers can aim to test whether the replication effect is smaller than that

title: Bayesian sample size planning for replications
guidance: BayesRepDesign (R) incorporates external knowledge into design; Micheloud and Held (2022) incorporate the original's uncertainty into power. Sequential testing with interim analyses can stop early. If using Bayes factors, use plausibly narrow priors, as wide priors (e.g., N(0,1)) may unfairly favour the null.
action: If using Bayes factors, justify a plausibly narrow prior and consider BayesRepDesign for planning.
quote: when planning to use Bayes Factors to make inferences about replication success, it is important to plan to use plausibly narrow priors

title: Use meta-analytic estimates carefully
guidance: Pool effect sizes from other studies in a multistudy paper or research programme for a more precise estimate. If using a meta-analysis, prioritise estimates corrected for publication bias and QRPs, and choose effects from studies resembling your planned design; metabus.org helps for correlational effects.
action: Base your target effect on bias-corrected meta-analytic estimates from similar designs where available.
quote: should prioritise estimates that aim to correct for publication bias and other QRPs

title: Recreate unspecified materials with theory in mind
guidance: If a key element is unspecified, ask the original authors. If they cannot be reached or cannot share, create new materials, paying attention to theory so they show face and construct validity.
action: Request missing materials; if unavailable, create new ones and document their validity rationale.
quote: new materials must be created. In this case, special attention should be paid to the theory, so that the new materials exhibit both face and construct validity

title: Update deprecated stimuli and state assumptions
guidance: Old stimuli (e.g., a 1987 car priced in German Marks) may no longer function the same. Originals rarely specify what a replacement stimulus must satisfy, so make your own assumptions about theoretical requirements and report them explicitly.
action: Identify outdated stimuli, replace them, and explicitly report your assumptions for the replacements.
quote: where they are not, replication authors need to make their own assumptions and report them explicitly

title: Test measurement invariance after translation
guidance: Translation standards vary: personality scales are usually validated with invariance tests, while social psychology often uses only back-translation. In any field, comparing effect sizes across samples requires measurement invariance, which should be tested rather than assumed where possible.
action: If translating measures, test measurement invariance rather than relying on back-translation alone.
quote: measurement invariance is required if one wants to compare effect sizes across samples, so that this should be tested rather than assumed where possible

title: Report original and state-of-the-art methods
guidance: Old apparatus or analysis methods may be outdated. Where possible report results from both the original and state-of-the-art methods; if you must choose, avoid invalid methods while keeping comparability. If adding extensions, consider order effects.
action: Plan to report results using both the original and a current analysis method.
quote: where possible, both the results from the original methods as well as state-of-the-art methods should be reported

title: Add checks to interpret null results
guidance: Replications carry uncertainty, so include checks that help interpret results, especially negative ones: positive or negative controls, manipulation checks (usually after critical parts), and attention checks.
action: Add manipulation, attention, and positive/negative control checks to your design.
quote: it is wise to include checks that will be helpful to interpret the results, especially if they are negative

title: Never derive effect sizes from small pilots
guidance: Pilot when resources are high or materials are new, but not as an underpowered version of the study. Use pilots to find methodological flaws or test assumptions; small pilots are too imprecise for power analyses. A few pilot participants plus a debriefing survey can check instructions, procedure and data recording.
action: Pilot with a few participants to check procedure and data recording, not effect size.
quote: small pilot studies should never be used to derive effect sizes for power analyses as their results are too imprecise

title: Involving original authors: mixed evidence
guidance: Evidence on whether involving original authors changes replication outcomes is mixed. In Many Labs 5, protocols revised after original-author feedback yielded effects similar to the earlier protocols, and Many Labs 4 found no overall effect of author involvement, whereas a review of social priming replications found author involvement was the strongest predictor of success. Invite author input to strengthen your design, but do not expect it to guarantee or rule out any particular result.
action: Decide and document whether and how original authors will be involved in reviewing your protocol.
quote: the strongest predictor of replication success was whether or not the replication team included at least one of the authors of the original paper

title: Consider adversarial collaboration or red teams
guidance: If your replication touches a contested finding, consider an adversarial collaboration, in which researchers with opposing views jointly design a study intended to settle the debate. A lighter alternative is a 'red team': outside experts critique your analysis plan without becoming authors, so they have no stake in a particular result.
action: Consider inviting critics or a red team to review your design and analysis plan before data collection.
quote: groups of researchers can collaborate and try to settle conflicting views by designing and conducting a study designed to settle a debate

title: Follow the original analysis plan closely
guidance: Your confirmatory analysis should mirror the original as closely as possible. This covers the statistical tests and also data processing steps such as outlier exclusion and how variables are transformed and computed. Replication analyses are often a mix of the original analysis and current best practice, so be explicit about which parts come from where.
action: List the original data-processing and statistical steps and replicate each one in your confirmatory analysis.
quote: replication studies should follow the original analysis plan as closely as possible. That does not only concern statistical procedures but also data processing

title: Screen raw data for careless responding
guidance: Even when you follow the original analysis, inspect your raw data for distributional anomalies that suggest inattention, guessing or speeding. Check theory-agnostic manipulation or condition checks (e.g., were people faster in a speed-focused condition?), attention checks and control trials. The handbook advises generally not removing participants from the main analysis on this basis: confirm that non-compliance rates are acceptably low and report robustness to excluding them.
action: Screen for inattention; report non-compliance rates and robustness rather than silently excluding.
quote: examine their raw data to check for distributional anomalies to detect whether participants might be inattentive, guessing or speeding

title: Do not silently drop inattentive participants
guidance: The handbook advises against removing participants from the main analysis on the basis of attention or compliance checks. Instead, show that non-compliance rates are acceptably low and report whether results hold when those participants are excluded. Ward and Meade (2023) review ways to assess and handle careless responding.
action: Report non-compliance rates and a robustness analysis excluding non-compliant participants.
quote: it is advisable not to remove participants from the main analysis on that basis, but instead to confirm that the rates of non-compliance are acceptably low

title: Run both the original and an updated test
guidance: If methodological advances suggest the original test was not robust, run the original test (for comparability) and the analysis most appropriate by current standards, such as both a t-test and a mixed-effects model. If you can get the original data, you may also re-run the updated analysis on it, which makes interpreting the comparison easier.
action: Preregister both the original statistical test and a state-of-the-art analysis where they differ.
quote: researchers may want to run both the test that the original study used, as well as the statistical approach that is most appropriate by today’s standards

title: Flawed original analyses cannot confer success
guidance: Sometimes the original analysis is fundamentally flawed; for example, the Dunning-Kruger effect has been shown to be strongly influenced by regression to the mean. You may report results from the original method alongside more robust tests, but frame them so that 'replication success' is not claimed when there is no evidence for the original claim.
action: Check whether the original analysis has known artefacts and frame any original-method results cautiously.
quote: needs to be very careful to frame them in a way that “replication success” cannot be claimed in the absence of evidence for the original claim

title: Preregister one central exclusion rule
guidance: Original exclusion criteria may conflict with current best practice. Running the analysis both ways is a sensible robustness check, but you must preregister one of the options as the central analysis so the choice is not made after seeing the data.
action: Preregister which exclusion criteria define the central analysis and which are robustness checks.
quote: it makes sense to run the analysis both ways to check for robustness, yet one analysis choice should be preregistered as the central analysis

title: Compare original and replication results directly
guidance: Always compare your results with the original ones; the method depends on your chosen success criterion. Unstandardized values, such as overall reaction times, are also informative because they reveal differences in sample characteristics between the studies.
action: Report original and replication estimates side by side, including relevant unstandardized values.
quote: Unstandardized values can be informative with respect to sample characteristics (e.g., overall reaction times).

title: No consensus on replication success
guidance: There is no strong consensus on what counts as replication success, and some approaches are biased or imprecise. As with significance testing, you face a trade-off between forcing a continuous outcome into success versus failure and making a clear decision. Choose and justify your criterion in advance rather than after seeing the results.
action: Choose and justify your replication-success criterion before data collection.
quote: There is no strong consensus yet on what constitutes a replication success and some approaches can be biased

title: Specify primary effects and how to aggregate
guidance: When a study yields several effects, results may be mixed, with some matching the original and some not. In your preregistration, state which effects are of primary interest and how you will combine results into an overall conclusion. Remember that requiring several effects to all replicate reduces statistical power.
action: Preregister the primary effect(s) and the rule for aggregating multiple results into one verdict.
quote: it is important for replication researchers to specify which effects are of primary interest in their preregistration, and how they will aggregate results

title: Menu of replication-success metrics (Heyard et al.)
guidance: The handbook reproduces an excerpt of Heyard et al.'s (2025) scoping review of metrics for quantifying reproducibility (Table 7.1). Each metric answers a different question, such as significance, effect-size difference, Bayes factors, intervals, small telescopes, equivalence and meta-analysis. Use the table to pick the metric that matches the question you actually want to answer, and consult the original paper for full descriptions.
action: Use the Heyard et al. (2025) table to match a success metric to your research question.
quote: Below, we present different approaches to assessing replication success as summarized by Heyard et al. (2025

title: Significance criterion
guidance: The simplest criterion asks whether both the original and the replication find a statistically significant effect in the same direction. It is widely used and applies across reproduction and replication types, but it dichotomizes the outcome, so consider pairing it with an effect-size-based criterion.
action: If using the significance criterion, also state the required direction of the effect.
quote: “Do the original and replication study both find a

title: Confidence and prediction interval criteria
guidance: Interval-based criteria include checking whether the replication effect falls within the original 95% confidence interval, and whether it falls within a 95% prediction interval that accounts for sampling variation in both studies. The prediction interval asks whether the replication estimates are statistically consistent with the original estimates.
action: Decide whether you will use a confidence or a prediction interval criterion and justify the choice.
quote: “Do the findings from the replication study align

title: Small telescopes criterion
guidance: The small telescopes approach (Simonsohn, 2015) asks whether the replication result is consistent with an effect large enough for the original study to have detected it. It helps judge whether the original study could have credibly found the effect it reported.
action: Consider a small-telescopes test and define the effect size the original could detect (e.g., 33% power).
quote: Criteria to operationalize replication success (excerpt from Heyard et al., 2025 [Table 4])

title: Equivalence and minimum-effect testing
guidance: When the original finding was a null result, equivalence testing asks whether the replication finds an effect that is equally negligible. Minimum effect testing asks whether the replication effect differs significantly from the smallest effect size needed to support the original claim. Both require you to specify a smallest effect size of interest in advance.
action: Define a smallest effect size of interest if you plan equivalence or minimum-effect tests.
quote: “For the replication of an original null finding,

title: Weigh all four validities when replications fail
guidance: A failed replication may point to statistical conclusion validity problems in the original study, but it can also reflect problems with internal, external or construct validity in either the original or the replication. Critically discuss methodological shortcomings of both studies before drawing conclusions about the robustness or generalizability of the original finding.
action: Discuss statistical, internal, external and construct validity of both studies in your discussion.
quote: other explanations need to be considered, including issues with internal, external, and construct validity in both original and replication studies

title: Unvalidated measures threaten interpretation
guidance: Construct validity is threatened when either study uses unvalidated ad-hoc measures, lacks validated manipulations, or when sample differences mean measures and manipulations no longer work as intended. Internal validity can also suffer, for example when attrition differs between conditions. Check these threats in your own design, not only in the original.
action: Check that your measures and manipulations are validated and work as intended in your sample.
quote: Construct validity is threatened when original or replication studies use unvalidated ad-hoc measures, fail to employ validated manipulations of the target construct

title: Move beyond vague hidden-moderator claims
guidance: Unknown or 'hidden' moderators, ranging from lab brightness to cultural differences, can influence results, and they are often used to dismiss unwelcome replication results. The same argument could cast doubt on any original study, so a skeptic who stops there is not taken seriously. Discuss concrete, theory-based candidate moderators instead.
action: Name specific, theoretically plausible moderators rather than appealing to unknown ones.
quote: it is important to move conversations about replication failure beyond general suspicion of hidden moderators

title: A single replication is never conclusive
guidance: Hidden moderators mean that one replication is never entirely conclusive, although it can raise enough doubt to question further investment. A failure shows that the original claim does not generalize to the replication's setting; whether it also calls the original setting into question must be argued on theoretical grounds.
action: Frame conclusions as applying to your replication setting and justify any broader claims with theory.
quote: Replication failure indicates that the original claim does not generalise to the setting of the replication.

title: Discuss every deviation and its likely impact
guidance: Evaluate each replication outcome in light of how close the replication was. Discuss all deviations, the reasons for them and, where possible, their potential impact on results. Use existing theory to judge whether a deviation should matter; for instance, most psychological theories are agnostic to age, so a different age distribution is usually unproblematic.
action: For each deviation, record the reason and a theory-based judgment of its likely impact.
quote: all deviations with the respective reasons and, if possible, their potential impact on the results should be discussed

title: Inductive versus deductive interpretation
guidance: How you interpret a result depends on your view. An inductive, phenomenon-oriented view assumes minimal generalizability, so only a highly similar replication can cast doubt on the original finding. A deductive, theory-oriented view assumes a theory is maximally general, so any failure casts doubt on the theory regardless of replication type. Consider interpreting your results from both views.
action: State whether you interpret your results from an inductive view, a deductive view, or both.
quote: Deductive or theory-oriented views assume maximal generality of a theory.

title: Invite original authors to comment
guidance: If your results do not match the original, you can ask the original authors for a comment to publish alongside your replication report; the appendix has a template. Some journals, such as the Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, require such statements at submission.
action: Send original authors your results and invite a comment for publication alongside your report.
quote: replication researchers can reach out to the original study’s authors and ask for a comment that they can publish together with the replication report

title: Follow transparency and reporting standards
guidance: Follow the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) guidelines and your field's reporting standards, such as the APA JARS standards for replications in psychology. Link your preregistration, analysis plan and analysis script, share all materials and data under an open license where ethical and legal limits allow, and report methods and results in full.
action: Link preregistration, analysis plan and script, and share materials and data under an open license.
quote: they should report a link to the preregistration, analysis plan, and analysis script, share all materials and data

title: Use descriptive, impersonal language
guidance: A failed replication can harm the original authors' reputation, so write descriptively and impersonally. When criticizing poor documentation, unavailable data or brief methods sections, keep the historical context in mind; sharing data was much harder in the 1990s and was not required in many fields until recently.
action: Review your manuscript for personal or accusatory wording about the original authors.
quote: We recommend a descriptive and impersonal language. When criticizing bad documentation, no access to data, or brevity in methods replication authors should keep in mind the historical context

title: Log results in FReD and PubPeer
guidance: Beyond a paper, make your result visible. Enter it in the FORRT Replication Database (FReD) through its guided survey, and post a comment on the original study on PubPeer describing the outcome with links or DOIs. Readers using the PubPeer browser plug-in will then see that a replication exists. These options can be combined with formal publication.
action: Submit your result to the FORRT Replication Database and post a PubPeer comment on the original.
quote: Researchers can comment on the original study and say that there is a replication attempt, describe the outcome, and provide links/references/DOIs to the replication(s).

title: Manuscript templates for replications
guidance: Templates exist for writing up your study: the I4R Replication Report Template for reproducibility analyses, the Standardized Reproduction and Replication Templates (StaRT) by Röseler et al. (2025) for reproductions and replications in general, and examples from Feldman (2024) for judgment and decision-making research.
action: Pick a report template (e.g., StaRT or I4R) before you start writing.
quote: For reproducibility analyses the I4R Replication Report Template (https://osf.io/j2qrx) can be used.

title: Post a preprint and seek suitable venues
guidance: The handbook recommends posting your report as a preprint so it is open access, visible, citable and open to comment, though preprints are usually not peer-reviewed. Many journals are not (yet) interested in replications, so consider journals dedicated to replications, or submit your preprint to a Peer Community In (PCI) community for peer review; several journals are PCI-friendly.
action: Post a preprint and shortlist replication-friendly journals or a PCI community.
quote: We recommend publishing a report in the form of a traditional or standardized manuscript as a preprint.

title: Journals dedicated to replications
guidance: Table 8.2 lists active journals dedicated to reproductions and replications, including Replication Research, the Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, ReScience C/X, the Journal of Robustness Reports, the Journal of Reproducibility in Neuroscience, the Journal of Management Scientific Reports and AIS Transactions on Replication Research. Many are diamond open access. Check each journal's disciplines and accepted article types. Institutions also often recommend adding a CC-BY statement to submissions.
action: Check Table 8.2 for a dedicated replication journal that fits your discipline and article type.
quote: Many institutions and libraries recommend adding a CC-BY disclaimer on journal submissions

title: Neuroimaging pipelines multiply researcher choices
guidance: In MRI research, preprocessing (motion correction, normalization, smoothing, filtering) and analysis offer many options, and different toolboxes or teams can reach different conclusions from the same data; in one study, 70 teams analyzing one dataset all used different pipelines. For neuroimaging replications, use automated preprocessing pipelines, ideally in containerized environments, and publish your scripts.
action: Fix and document the full preprocessing and analysis pipeline, including software versions.
quote: different teams analyzing the same dataset can arrive at different final conclusions dependent on the used pipeline

title: Power in MRI replications is hard to justify
guidance: Power analysis is hard in MRI because of the mass-univariate, three-dimensional data structure, and it is rarely done. Large studies suggest brain-wide effects in mental health are very small and may require thousands of participants, while most MRI studies are small and likely underpowered. Smaller samples may suffice where larger effects are expected or when using within-subject or individually tailored designs.
action: Justify your MRI sample size against realistic, likely small, effect sizes.
quote: most MRI studies tend to have small sample sizes, making them likely underpowered

title: Define where in the brain success counts
guidance: For voxel-based MRI replications, you must define where in the brain the success criterion applies: at the original peak voxel, in a sphere around it (e.g., 15 mm), in the anatomical region where the effect was found, or in the original thresholded mask. Each option has limitations, so you may need to combine criteria, and your preregistration should spell out the spatial definition.
action: Preregister the spatial definition (peak, sphere, anatomical ROI or mask) of replication success.
quote: it has to be defined where in the brain the criteria of replication success should be met

title: Checklist 1: Justify choice of target study and claims
guidance: Item 1 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Explain why this study and these specific claims deserve replication.
action: Write a justification for your target study and the specific claims tested.
quote: Justify choice of target study and claims

title: Checklist 2: Choose a replication type that fits your aims
guidance: Item 2 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Pick the reproduction or replication type (e.g., close or conceptual) that matches what you want to learn.
action: State your aim and the reproduction/replication type that aligns with it.
quote: Choose a reproduction/replication type that aligns with your aims

title: Checklist 3: Gather and review all relevant materials
guidance: Item 3 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Collect the original materials, data and code, and read them carefully before designing your study.
action: Collect and review all original materials, data and code.
quote: Gather and review all relevant materials

title: Checklist 4: Reproduce before you replicate
guidance: Item 4 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Where the original data allow, first check that you can reproduce the original results before collecting new data.
action: Attempt to reproduce the original results from the original data before replicating.
quote: Reproduce before you replicate, where possible

title: Checklist 5: Discuss all changes to original materials
guidance: Item 5 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Discuss every update, change and extension to the original materials, keeping the replication as close as possible and only as updated as necessary.
action: Document and justify every update, change and extension to the original materials.
quote: Discuss all updates, changes, and extensions of the original materials (as close as possible, as updated as necessary)

title: Checklist 6: Preregister study and analysis plan
guidance: Item 6 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Register your study design and analysis plan before collecting data.
action: Preregister your study and analysis plan before data collection.
quote: Preregister your study and analysis plan

title: Checklist 7: Predetermine success and failure conditions
guidance: Item 7 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Decide in advance what results will count as replication success and failure.
action: Specify success and failure conditions before seeing the data.
quote: Predetermine conditions for success and failure

title: Checklist 8: Use balanced language about outcomes
guidance: Item 8 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Describe outcomes in balanced, non-sensational language, whether the replication succeeded or failed.
action: Check your write-up for balanced language when describing outcomes.
quote: Use balanced language when describing the outcomes

title: Checklist 9: Evaluate outcomes and reasons for divergence
guidance: Item 9 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Carefully evaluate your results and discuss possible reasons for any divergence from the original.
action: Discuss potential reasons for any divergence between original and replication results.
quote: Carefully evaluate outcomes and potential reasons for divergences

title: Checklist 10: Report comprehensively and openly
guidance: Item 10 of the handbook's 10-item reproduction and replication checklist. Report your research in full and make it openly accessible.
action: Make your full report, materials and data openly accessible.
quote: Report your research comprehensively and openly accessible

title: Email: requesting materials and data
guidance: Address the original authors by name and explain that you are replicating their research, naming the phenomenon and study and briefly saying why it matters. List exactly which materials, data and code you need so you can design a replication as close as possible to the original, cite the original study, and close politely.
action: Email original authors a specific list of materials, data and code, with the study citation.
quote: Can you please send us the following materials to help us design a replication as close as possible to your original study?

title: Email: feedback on your replication paradigm
guidance: Tell the original authors which study you plan to replicate and why, and share a link to a mock-up of your paradigm. Ask whether it accurately captures their design and invite comments on any details that differ. State your planned sample, and if it differs from the original population, acknowledge the deviation and say you will note it prominently in any write-up.
action: Send original authors a link to your paradigm mock-up and ask about differences from their study.
quote: I’m writing to share a mock-up of the replication to get your feedback on whether this paradigm accurately captures the design of your study.

title: Email: inviting comment on replication results
guidance: Tell the original authors which study you replicated and summarize your results. Offer them the chance to comment, explain where you plan to publish (e.g., a venue that asks for original-author comments) and say that any comment will be part of the report. Include the citation of the original study and a link to, or attachment of, your replication report.
action: Email original authors your results and report, inviting an optional comment for publication.
quote: We want to provide you with an opportunity to comment on these findings.

title: What a close replication is
guidance: Brandt et al. use 'close replication' rather than 'exact' or 'direct' because no psychology study can ever be recreated perfectly. The aim is to reproduce the original methods and procedures as faithfully as possible, so that ideally the only remaining differences are unavoidable ones such as a different set of participants. Frame your project in these terms and expect some differences to be inevitable.
action: Describe your study as a close replication and list the differences you cannot avoid.
quote: close replication studies aim to recreate a study as closely as

title: The five ingredients of a convincing replication
guidance: A convincing close replication is carried out rigorously, ideally by independent researchers, and has five ingredients: (1) carefully define the effect and methods you will replicate; (2) follow the original methods as exactly as possible; (3) have high statistical power; (4) make complete details of the replication available; (5) evaluate the results and compare them critically with the original. The paper's 36 questions work as a checklist for planning and reporting against these ingredients.
action: Check your replication plan against all five Replication Recipe ingredients.
quote: A convincing close replication par excellence is executed rigorously

title: Not every study is worth replicating
guidance: Before you commit resources, justify why this particular effect should be replicated (Recipe Question 2). Brandt et al. base this on the effect's theoretical importance to the field or its direct or indirect value to society. Also consider how much confidence already exists: an effect that already has several close replications may be less urgent to replicate than one with none.
action: Write a short justification of the effect's theoretical/societal importance and its existing replication record.
quote: By considering the theoretical and practical importance of a ﬁnding

title: Pin down the exact effect of interest
guidance: Decide at the very start exactly which effect you are replicating, because this choice drives almost every later design decision. In complex designs the effect may be only part of the results; for example, in a 2 x 2 cross-over design it could be the interaction, both simple effects, or just one simple effect. Write a verbal description of the target effect (Recipe Question 1).
action: State in one sentence the precise effect (e.g., interaction vs. a specific simple effect) you will replicate.
quote: know the precise effect of interest from the beginning of the

title: Record the original effect and study context
guidance: Recipe Questions 3–9 ask you to write down the original effect size, its confidence interval, the original sample size, where the study was run (lab, field, online), the country or region, the kind of sample (e.g., students, MTurk, representative), and the mode of administration (paper, computer, other). Brandt et al. note that when such methodological details are unclear, you may need to ask the original authors or make an informed guess.
action: Fill in original effect size, CI, N, setting, country, sample type and administration mode.
quote: What kind of sample did the original study use? (e.g., student, Mturk, representative)

title: Start by contacting the original authors
guidance: To follow the original methods as exactly as possible, begin by asking the original authors for their materials (Recipe Question 10). If they are not available, check whether the materials exist elsewhere, such as previously published scales, and record how any materials you had to create were built. Where feasible, work with the original authors; the authors note that much of the Recipe is easier with their cooperation.
action: Email the original authors requesting all study materials, and log their response.
quote: with contacting the original authors of the study to try and obtain the

title: When original materials cannot be obtained
guidance: If the original authors are uncooperative or cannot be reached, rebuild the methods as well as you can from the original methods section, assuming the original study was highly rigorous. Fill any gaps using best practice for that paradigm (e.g., for a lexical decision task), and ask expert colleagues in the area whether your version faithfully recreates the study as described. Brandt et al. say replications should still go ahead when collaboration is not possible.
action: Document every reconstructed material and get feedback from an expert in the paradigm.
quote: should be recreated to the best of the replicator researchers' ability,

title: Adapt culture-bound materials for functional equivalence
guidance: Some materials are tied to a particular time or culture (e.g., a specific election or sporting event) and will not mean the same thing to your participants. In those cases the most valid replication may change the stimuli so they are functionally equivalent, ideally developed with the original authors and with input from the research community. Depending on how large the change is, run a pilot to test that the manipulations and measures capture the same constructs, and justify your assumptions (Recipe Question 11).
action: Pilot-test any adapted stimuli for equivalence and write down why their meaning holds.
quote: changing the stimulus materials to ensure that they are functionally

title: Same code does not guarantee same experience
guidance: Technical details such as monitor type or settings, or the input device (keyboard vs. response box), can change how accurately a manipulation is delivered or a response is measured. For instance, the same presentation time can be subliminal on one monitor and supraliminal on another. Check that participants actually experience the stimuli as the original participants did, instead of assuming that reusing the original program is enough.
action: Verify timing and display properties of your hardware against the original setup.
quote: not necessarily be enough to replicate the experience of the stimuli by

title: Document key design choices (Questions 10–16)
guidance: The 'Designing the Replication Study' section of the Recipe asks where your materials came from, how you know the original assumptions (e.g., the meaning of the stimuli) hold in your setting, where the experimenter is during data collection, whether the experimenter knows participants' conditions and the overall hypotheses, and your target sample size and its rationale. Answering these up front makes your design transparent to reviewers.
action: Answer Recipe Questions 10–16, including experimenter location and blinding.
quote: 11. I know that assumptions (e.g., about the meaning of the stimuli) in the original study

title: Aim for high statistical power
guidance: An underpowered replication may wrongly suggest the original effect was a false positive. Brandt et al. note recommendations of at least .80 and up to .95 power, and because published effect sizes are likely overestimates, you should err towards higher power. For complex designs, consult the power and sample-size planning literature. If several replications already exist, base the calculation on the average meta-analytic effect size, and consider pooling participants with other labs if you cannot recruit enough.
action: Run a power analysis targeting at least .80 (preferably higher) and record the rationale.
quote: recommended that a sufﬁcient amount of statistical power is at least

title: The 2.5 × original sample size rule
guidance: Power calculations are one way to justify your sample size, but Brandt et al. also mention Simonsohn's (2013) alternative: use 2.5 times the original sample size. Whichever rule you use, report it as your sample-size rationale (Recipe Questions 15–16).
action: Compute 2.5 × the original N and compare it with your power-based target.
quote: that an alternative for determining sample sizes is to take 2.5 times

title: Rate each component Exact, Close, or Different
guidance: For the instructions, measures, stimuli, procedure, location, remuneration and participant population (Recipe Questions 17–23), rate your study as exact, close, or conceptually different from the original, and justify each rating. This lets reviewers judge whether deviations were justified, shows where your study sits on the close-to-conceptual continuum, and helps later work identify boundary conditions once several replications exist.
action: Complete an Exact/Close/Different rating with justification for all seven components.
quote: For each part of the study indicate whether the replication study is Exact, Close, or Conceptually Different

title: Anticipate and test influential differences
guidance: Identify differences between your study and the original that might change the size or direction of the effect (Recipe Question 24), such as participants' socioeconomic status or mood at the time of testing. Measure such a variable at the end of the study so it does not interfere with the close replication, then test it as a moderator within your sample (Question 25).
action: List likely moderators and add end-of-study measures to test them.
quote: at the end of the replication study so as to not interfere with the close

title: Handling 'improvements' to the original method
guidance: If you are tempted to improve the original study (e.g., use a newer version of a scale), the authors suggest doing so in consultation with the original authors and explaining why. The most informative option is to run both the original and improved methods, either as two replications or by randomly assigning participants to the original or improved version as an experimental factor.
action: If changing a method, randomize participants to the original vs. improved version.
quote: study as a randomized experimental factor so that participants are randomly assigned to

title: Preregister to protect your success criteria
guidance: Preregister the replication's methods (Questions 10–16, 25), its differences from the original (17–24), and its planned analysis and evaluation (26–28). Working as openly as is ethically possible guards against adjusting success criteria after the fact, makes your work easier to evaluate, and limits flexibility in choosing analyses.
action: Preregister methods, differences and the analysis/evaluation plan before data collection.
quote: inoculates against post hoc adjustment of replication success criteria,

title: Use the OSF Replication Recipe templates
guidance: The 36 questions are built into the Open Science Framework as a replication template. Choose the Replication Recipe Pre-Registration template to answer the planning questions in a read-only, time-stamped file, and after the study use the Post-Completion registration to answer the rest. Include links to both in your submitted paper.
action: Register your plan with the OSF Replication Recipe Pre-Registration template.
quote: the Open Science Framework as a replication template (see Fig. 1).

title: Fix exclusions, analysis plan, and success definition
guidance: Before data collection, write down your exclusion criteria, such as outlier handling (Question 26), and your analysis plan, justifying any differences from the original analysis (Question 27). Also define in advance what counts as a successful replication (Question 28).
action: Write your exclusion rules, analysis plan, and success definition before collecting data.
quote: 27. My analysis plan is (justify differences from the original):

title: Report two tests, not just significance
guidance: Calling a replication a 'success' or 'failure' only because p < .05 is not enough. Calculate the replication effect size and its confidence interval (Questions 30–31) and test (1) whether the effect differs from zero and (2) whether it differs statistically from the original effect size (Question 32).
action: Report the replication effect size, its CI, and a test against the original effect size.
quote: Evaluating the replication should involve reporting two tests: 1) the

title: Four possible replication verdicts
guidance: Based on the two tests, Brandt et al. (following Simonsohn, 2013) distinguish four outcomes. Success: different from zero and similar to or larger than the original, in the same direction. Informative failure: not different from zero or in the opposite direction, and significantly different from the original. Practical failure: significantly different from both zero and the original. Inconclusive: different from neither. State your verdict and your reasons (Question 33).
action: Classify your result into one of the four verdicts and justify it.
quote: (both signiﬁcantly different from the null and from the original), or

title: Aggregate meta-analytically and weigh all evidence
guidance: Consider combining your effect with the original and any other close replications in a meta-analysis, and judge the total weight of evidence rather than a single result. The authors note that a high-quality, higher-powered replication will often carry more weight than a lower-powered original. Discuss limitations of both studies, including Type I and Type II errors and random variation in effect size (Question 36).
action: Run a small meta-analysis combining the original, your study, and existing close replications.
quote: analytic aggregation of the replication study's effect with the original

title: Don't use context as an untested excuse
guidance: Contextual factors such as sample characteristics, room temperature, or equipment can plausibly affect results, but do not use them after the fact as untested explanations for why an effect failed to replicate. Instead, carefully test whether a specific contextual feature reliably affects the result and whether it explains the difference.
action: Label any contextual explanation for discrepancies as a hypothesis for future tests.
quote: should not be used defensively as untested post-hoc justiﬁcations

title: Share data, syntax, and all analyses
guidance: After the study, make your data, analysis syntax, and all analyses available so others can fully evaluate the replication and test alternative explanations (Questions 34–35). Exceptions can be made for data protection, e.g., data that are hard to anonymize. The authors suggest the Open Science Framework for sharing.
action: Post data, analysis scripts, and full results to a public repository (e.g., OSF).
quote: the data, analysis syntax, and all analyses should be made available so

title: A failed replication is not an accusation
guidance: Science works with probabilities, so some unsuccessful replications are expected. A failure does not necessarily mean the original finding is wrong or fraudulent. Avoid a 'score-keeping' framing (e.g., 2 failures vs. 1 success); take a meta-analytic view, and treat careful records of differences as clues to the processes behind the effect.
action: Check your discussion for score-keeping language and frame the results cumulatively.
quote: Fifth, a replication failure does not necessarily mean that the original

title: Close replication will not fix original confounds
guidance: A close replication inherits any confounds or theoretical limitations of the original design. To remove confounds or extend generalizability, add conceptual replications or replication-plus-extension designs. When your interest is a theoretical prediction rather than an effect in one paradigm, a mix of close and conceptual replications builds the most confidence.
action: Note known confounds in the original and decide whether to add an extension or conceptual study.
quote: of close and conceptual replications is the best way to build conﬁdence

title: Use the Recipe as a teaching checklist
guidance: The authors present the Replication Recipe as a set of standard criteria that researchers, teachers, and students can use to carry out meaningful replications and build them into their academic habits. Mentors can have students work through the 36 questions to plan, preregister, and report a replication.
action: Have students complete the 36-question Recipe for their target study.
quote: Our Replication Recipe can be used by researchers, teachers, and

title: 'Significant vs. nonsignificant' is a flawed replication test
guidance: A common rule declares a 'failure to replicate' when the original was significant and the follow-up is not. Bonett explains that this rule is logically flawed: failing to reject the null in the follow-up does not show the effect is zero. Do not use this rule as your success criterion.
action: Remove any significance-only success criterion from your plan.
quote: This significance-based criterion for assessing replication is logically flawed

title: Don't just check if your CI covers the original estimate
guidance: Another common criterion calls a replication a failure if the follow-up confidence interval excludes the original point estimate. This ignores the fact that the original estimate has its own sampling error. Compare the two studies using a confidence interval for the difference between the effect sizes instead.
action: Base comparisons on a CI for the difference between original and follow-up effects.
quote: flawed because the sampling error of the effect size in the original study is ignored.

title: What counts as a comparable follow-up study
guidance: Bonett defines a comparable (direct) follow-up study as one that (a) samples from a population believed to be similar to the original, (b) uses the same research design and treatment conditions, (c) estimates the same type of effect-size parameter with the same control variables, and (d) uses the same measurement scales. His replication criteria assume a comparable follow-up.
action: Confirm your study meets criteria (a)–(d) for a comparable follow-up study.
quote: research design and includes the same treatment conditions as in the original study

title: When a different measurement scale is acceptable
guidance: For a direct ('comparable') replication whose results you will compare with the original using Bonett's confidence-interval criteria, you should use the original measurement scales. Bonett says this requirement can be cautiously relaxed only if both studies measure exactly the same construct, the two scales are linearly related, and a standardized effect size is used.
action: If changing a scale, justify same construct, linear relation, and a standardized effect size.
quote: relaxed if the two studies measure the exact same construct, the measurement scales in the original

title: Rebuild the original CI from reported statistics
guidance: You need a confidence interval for the original effect, built from its estimate and standard error. If the standard error was not reported, it can usually be computed from other reported information, such as SDs and group sizes for mean differences, or the correlation and N for a Pearson correlation. The paper's R functions compute these intervals from summary statistics alone.
action: Compute the original effect's standard error and CI from reported summary statistics.
quote: If the standard error of the estimate has not been reported, it is usually possible to compute the standard error using other reported information.

title: Treat nonsignificant results as inconclusive
guidance: Use the confidence interval for directional two-sided tests. If the upper limit is below 0, conclude the effect is negative; if the lower limit is above 0, conclude it is positive; otherwise the result is inconclusive, not evidence that the effect is zero. The same logic applies to the CI for the difference between the original and follow-up effects.
action: Report CI-based direction decisions and describe CIs that include 0 as inconclusive.
quote: It is important to remember that a nonsignificant result should not be interpreted as evidence that H0 is true.

title: Test similarity with an equivalence test (ROPE)
guidance: To show that the original and follow-up effects are similar, use an equivalence test. Choose h, a difference small enough to be unimportant, which defines a range of practical equivalence (ROPE) from –h to h. If the CI for the difference falls entirely inside the ROPE, the effects are equivalent; if it falls entirely outside, they differ meaningfully; otherwise the result is inconclusive. A 100(1 – 2α)% CI (e.g., 90%) is typically used.
action: Preregister h (your ROPE) and use a 90% CI for the difference to test equivalence.
quote: h is called the range of practical equivalence (ROPE). The value of h is chosen by the researcher to represent a small or unimportant difference

title: Choosing strict or liberal ROPE values
guidance: A strict ROPE is half the difference between a medium and a small effect, and a liberal ROPE is half the difference between a large and a small effect. For standardized mean differences this gives h = 0.15 (strict) or 0.3 (liberal); for log-odds ratios, 0.36 or 0.69. For correlations, base h on a .05 (strict) or .10 (liberal) difference in squared correlations (e.g., original r = .3 gives h ≈ .074 or .136). A strict ROPE is more convincing but can require very large samples.
action: Pick a strict or liberal h for your effect type and justify the choice.
quote: A strict ROPE could be defined as half the difference between a medium and small standardized mean difference

title: ROPE for unstandardized means on rating scales
guidance: For unstandardized mean differences or slopes, setting a ROPE takes subject-matter expertise. For averages of 5-point items, Bonett suggests treating 0.25/0.5/0.75 as small/medium/large, giving h = 0.125 (strict) or 0.25 (liberal). For 7-point items, scale these by 1.5, giving h = 0.1875 (strict) or 0.375 (liberal). The same logic works for 4- and 6-point scales.
action: Derive h from your response scale's range using the strict/liberal rule.
quote: The problem is often simplified in applications where the response variable is an average of 5-point questionnaire items.

title: Directional replication
guidance: Directional replication means both the original and follow-up confidence intervals exclude 0 and point in the same direction (both positive or both negative). It is the most basic form of replication evidence and requires a follow-up large enough to reject the null.
action: Check that both CIs exclude 0 in the same direction before claiming directional replication.
quote: To demonstrate directional replication, it is necessary to reject both null hypotheses

title: Strong effect-size replication
guidance: Strong effect-size replication is shown when the CI for the difference between the original and follow-up effects lies completely within the ROPE, so the two effects are practically equivalent. It is more convincing with a strict ROPE, but that usually requires very large samples in both studies. You control only the follow-up's sample size.
action: Test whether the CI for the effect difference lies entirely within your ROPE.
quote: Strong effect-size replication is more compelling with a strict ROPE than with a liberal ROPE, but a strict ROPE usually requires a very large sample size

title: Four types of nonreplication evidence
guidance: Bonett describes four types. Directional nonreplication: both CIs exclude 0 but point in opposite directions, which is usually serious. Strong effect-size nonreplication: the CI for the difference lies wholly outside the ROPE. Weak effect-size nonreplication: the CI for the difference excludes 0. Null effect-size nonreplication: the follow-up CI lies within –h2 to h2, a trivially small range. Directional or strong nonreplication implies weak nonreplication, so weak need not be reported separately in those cases.
action: Classify any nonreplication by type using Bonett's Table 2 criteria.
quote: Directional nonreplication is usually a serious form of nonreplication because the original study and the follow-up study support opposite conclusions.

title: Showing a null effect needs a very large sample
guidance: To show that the follow-up effect is trivially small, the whole CI must fall inside a narrow range around zero, which can require a large sample. The required sample size grows sharply as the true effect approaches the boundary. If this is your goal, plan the sample with that in mind or accept that it may not be realistic.
action: If aiming to show a null effect, set h2 and confirm your sample can achieve it.
quote: Obtaining null effect-size nonreplication evidence may not be a realistic goal in some replication studies.

title: Inconclusive is not 'failed to replicate'
guidance: If the original was significant but your follow-up CI includes 0, directional replication is inconclusive, not failed. Bonett notes that large replication projects often labeled such results as failures. Likewise, when the CI for the difference includes ±h, strong effect-size nonreplication is inconclusive and should not be called a failure.
action: Replace 'failed to replicate' with 'inconclusive' wherever your CI includes 0 or ±h.
quote: It is a common mistake to interpret inconclusive directional nonreplication as a “replication failure.”

title: Report equivalence together with inconclusive difference
guidance: You can obtain strong effect-size replication (difference CI within the ROPE) and inconclusive weak nonreplication (difference CI includes 0) at the same time. Report both, because together they show that the difference is within the equivalence range and could be very close to zero.
action: Report both the equivalence result and the zero-difference result for the effect difference.
quote: If strong effect-size replication is obtained along with inconclusive weak effect-size nonreplication evidence, it is informative to report both results

title: Explain nonreplication through moderators
guidance: Nonreplication does not necessarily mean the original was wrong or that your study was flawed. Population differences, or subtle differences in measurement, treatment, or testing environment, can moderate effect size. Make methodological and theory-based moderators the main focus of your discussion when you obtain nonreplication, and propose them for future research.
action: Discuss specific methodological and theoretical moderators that could explain any nonreplication.
quote: nonreplication results do not imply that the results of the original study are necessarily wrong or that the follow-up study was conducted inappropriately.

title: Combine studies with varying-coefficient methods
guidance: If there is no directional nonreplication, report a CI for the average of the two effects, (θ1 + θ2)/2. It is usually more precise than the original CI and generalizes to both study populations. Bonett recommends varying-coefficient meta-analysis (implemented in his R functions) rather than traditional fixed- or random-effects methods, whose assumptions will not hold with two studies.
action: Compute a varying-coefficient CI for the average of original and follow-up effects.
quote: The traditional fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analysis methods (Borenstein et al., 2009) should not be used

title: Sample size is the key design decision
guidance: Bonett calls follow-up sample size perhaps the most important design consideration, because too small a sample makes inconclusive results likely. For directional evidence, the follow-up must be large enough to reject the null with the desired power; the required N increases with smaller α, higher power, and smaller planning effect sizes.
action: Set α, desired power, and a planning effect size, then compute the required follow-up N.
