quote: If the sample size is too small, there is a high probability of obtaining inconclusive results.

title: Use a conservative effect-size planning value
guidance: The original estimate contains sampling error, so using it directly as the planning value can mislead. An alternative is the 80% one-sided lower confidence limit (for positive estimates), approximately the estimate − 0.84 × SE1. If SE1 was not reported, derive it from other reported statistics.
action: Compute estimate − 0.84×SE1 and use it as your planning effect size.
quote: An alternative approach is to use an 80% one-sided lower (for positive estimates) or upper (for negative estimates) confidence limit as the effect-size planning value.

title: Plan for precision, not only power
guidance: A replication is more informative when the follow-up CI is narrow. Plan sample size for a target CI width as well as for power. In Bonett's example (r = .21), a 95% CI width of .15 needs N = 625 and a width of .2 needs N = 352, while power of .8 or .9 for a directional test needs N = 176 or 235.
action: Compute N for your target CI width alongside N for your target power.
quote: Using .21 as the correlation planning value and setting the desired 95% confidence width to .15, the required sample size is 625.

title: A small original caps what you can show
guidance: The standard error of the difference between effects depends on both studies, so the CI for the difference can never be narrower than the original study's CI, however large your sample. If the original sample was small, strong effect-size replication may be impossible to show; check this before choosing that as your goal.
action: Check whether the original CI is narrow enough to allow an equivalence conclusion.
quote: If the sample size in the original study is too small, it may not be possible to obtain strong effect-size replication evidence.

title: R functions for replication analysis
guidance: Bonett's Supplement 1 provides R functions (Table 1), such as rep_mean2, rep_stdmean2, rep_cor, and rep_general, that compute CIs for the original effect, the follow-up effect, their difference, and their average from summary statistics. There are also functions for linear contrasts in k-group replication-extension designs and for odds ratios. Supplement 2 gives worked examples.
action: Download Bonett's Supplement 1 and run the rep_ function matching your effect size.
quote: using only summary information from the original and follow-up studies, are provided in the Supplementary Material

title: R functions for follow-up sample size
guidance: Table 4 of the paper lists R functions for planning the follow-up sample: size_ci_* functions for a desired CI width (means, standardized means, proportions, correlations, slopes), size_test_* functions for a directional test with desired power, and size_ci_diff for estimating the original–follow-up difference with a specified width.
action: Use size_test_* and size_ci_* functions to justify your follow-up sample size.
quote: Several R functions (Table 4) are provided in an Supplement File available in the online version of the journal

title: Consider a replication-extension design
guidance: A replication-extension design gives all the replication evidence described in the paper and adds new information about extra factors, factor levels, controls, moderators, or mediators. For example, you could include one sample matching the original population plus samples from other sectors to extend the findings. The extension part can be seen as a conceptual or constructive replication.
action: Decide whether to add an extension sample or factor alongside the direct replication.
quote: Replication-extension designs are attractive because they provide all of the replication and nonreplication evidence described here in addition to important new information

title: Don't generalize beyond the study population
guidance: Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals apply only to the population the sample was drawn from, yet findings are often written up as if they apply more broadly. Describe your follow-up's study population precisely and limit conclusions to it, or to both populations when you report the combined (average) effect.
action: Describe your study population explicitly and scope conclusions to it.
quote: hypothesis testing and interval estimation results apply only to the population (called the study population) from which the sample was randomly selected

title: Replication design and analysis must be taught
guidance: Bonett notes calls for more training in replication design and analysis, and argues that researchers need to learn specialized software because standard packages are built for single studies. Mentors should teach the formal replication criteria and R tools as a core research-design skill.
action: Include a session on Bonett's replication criteria and R functions in methods training.
quote: Standing et al. (2014) and Janz (2016) argued that more training in the design and analysis of replication research is needed.

title: Replication has more than one legitimate goal
guidance: Anderson and Maxwell argue that most replication studies judge success only by whether p < .05 comes out the same way as in the original. That is one goal among several. Before you design your study, ask what question your replication is really meant to answer: whether the effect exists, whether it is null, how big it is, or how it compares with the original.
action: Write down which of the six replication goals your study pursues.
quote: we argue that authors may be considering replication in an overly narrow context

title: Six replication goals, analyses and success criteria
guidance: The article's Table 1 pairs each goal with an analysis and a success criterion. (1) Show the effect exists: repeat the original analysis, success = p < .05. (2) Show a null effect: equivalence test, success = CI entirely inside the region of equivalence. (3) Estimate the effect size precisely: AIPE plus a CI for the effect size. (4) Combine with the original: CI for the average effect size. (5) Show clear inconsistency: CI for the difference in effect sizes excludes 0. (6) Show clear consistency: equivalence test on the difference in effect sizes.
action: Match your goal to its analysis and success criterion in Table 1.
quote: The following section introduces six potential goals for replication

title: Fix replication goals before analysing data
guidance: The six goals can be combined when your questions call for it, but you must choose them before you analyse the data. Picking a goal after seeing the results lets you pick whichever definition of success happens to fit. Put your goals and their success criteria in your preregistration.
action: Preregister each replication goal and its success criterion before data analysis.
quote: We caution that goals should be decided on a priori, before conducting analyses

title: Choose Goal 1 when existence and direction matter most
guidance: For a surprising or counterintuitive original finding, the key question may be whether the effect exists and points the same way, not how big it is. In that case the significance-based goal (Goal 1) is a sound choice. Say in your aims that effect size is secondary for your question.
action: Justify whether existence/direction or effect size is the key question for your target.
quote: Replications of results of this nature may simply need to reproduce a statistically significant effect in the intended direction

title: Goal 1: mirror the original analysis
guidance: If your goal is to show that the effect exists, choose an adequate sample size and then run the same kind of analysis as the original, such as a t test, regression or ANOVA. Take the original study's context into account when deciding exactly how to run it.
action: Specify the original study's exact analysis as your confirmatory test for Goal 1.
quote: the statistical methods chosen should typically mirror those in the original study

title: Goal 1 success needs the same direction
guidance: Under Goal 1, a significant result counts as a successful replication only if the effect points the same way as the original. A significant effect in the opposite direction is normally a failure. The authors note a few exceptions, where a theory only predicts some difference between conditions and not its direction.
action: Define success as p < .05 AND an effect in the original direction.
quote: it is often not only the statistical significance of the effect, but also the directionality inherent in the statistically significant finding that is important to convey

title: Nonsignificance is not evidence of no effect
guidance: Many published replications treat p > .05 as showing that the effect is absent, but a significance test cannot show that. If your analysis was built to detect an effect, describe a nonsignificant result as a failure to detect it, not as proof of a null. If you want to claim a null, use equivalence tests or Bayesian methods.
action: Never report p > .05 alone as evidence that the original effect is absent.
quote: failure to reject the null hypothesis does not necessarily constitute evidence that the null hypothesis should be accepted

title: Goal 2: flip the burden of proof for a null
guidance: If you are sceptical of the original and want to show the effect is null, a standard significance test is the wrong tool. The alternative hypothesis becomes the default, and your data must provide enough evidence to overturn it. The authors advise against simply reusing the original study's traditional analysis for this goal.
action: For a null claim, plan an equivalence test or Bayes factor, not the original test.
quote: when the goal is to infer a null effect, the alternative hypothesis should be the default hypothesis

title: Set the region of equivalence before data collection
guidance: The first step of an equivalence test (TOST) is to define a region of equivalence: effect values so small that you treat them as essentially zero. Base this range on theory, for example the smallest meaningful difference on the original scale. You must set it before you collect any replication data.
action: Preregister theory-based equivalence bounds (e.g., ±0.5 scale points) before collecting data.
quote: this interval is based entirely on theory and must be specified prior to collecting replication data

title: Run TOST with a 90% confidence interval
guidance: For TOST at alpha = .05, compute a 90% confidence interval (1 − 2α) around the replication estimate, not the usual 95%. You can conclude equivalence only if the whole interval lies inside the region of equivalence. A point estimate inside the region is not enough. In the authors' example the estimate was 0.2 with bounds of ±0.5, but the 90% CI ran from −0.25 to 0.65, so equivalence was not shown.
action: Compute the 90% CI and check it lies entirely within your equivalence bounds.
quote: if the confidence interval of the estimate falls entirely within the region of equivalence, the null hypothesis can be claimed to be functionally true

title: Bayes factors to quantify support for the null
guidance: Bayesian methods are an alternative way to support a null: the ROPE approach, and Bayes factors that compare how well the null and the alternative explain the data. For a two-group t test, an online calculator only needs the per-group n, the t value and the prior scale. Decide ahead of time how you will interpret the Bayes factor, because what counts as strong evidence can vary by subdiscipline.
action: If claiming a null, report a Bayes factor (with stated prior) alongside or instead of TOST.
quote: A second Bayesian method specifically quantifies the degree of support for the null hypothesis

title: Equivalence claims need large samples
guidance: To show that an effect is essentially zero, you need a more precise estimate than you need to just miss significance. Replications that aim for Goal 2 or Goal 6 therefore usually need much larger samples than the original. Plan your sample size for the width of the interval you will need.
action: Size your sample so the expected CI fits within your equivalence bounds.
quote: It should not be surprising that large sample sizes may be necessary, as it requires more precision to establish equivalence than it does to simply fail to reject the null

title: Power based on original effect sizes is inflated
guidance: Published effect sizes tend to be too large because of publication bias and sampling error. If you base your power analysis on the original effect size, your real power can be much lower than you planned. A study that reports power of .80 may in fact have much less. The authors point to Taylor and Muller (1996) for a power method that takes bias and uncertainty into account.
action: Adjust power analysis for bias/uncertainty in the original effect size estimate.
quote: even replication studies that claim to have power greater than .8 may have actual power that is much lower

title: The original study's n matters when comparing or combining
guidance: Under Goals 4, 5 and 6 you combine or compare your result with the original, so the original study's sample size affects how precise your conclusion can be. A small original study limits what even a large replication can show about differences or equivalence. Take this into account when you plan your sample.
action: Record the original sample size and factor it into precision/power planning.
quote: the sample size of the original study plays an important role anytime the goal involves either comparing or combining the results

title: Goal 3: plan sample size for precision (AIPE)
guidance: If you care about how big the effect is, use accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) to plan your sample. Choose n to reach a target confidence interval width, not a target power. For example, estimating d within a half-width of 0.15 took about 350 participants per group.
action: Set a target CI half-width and compute n with AIPE.
quote: This goal, accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE), is intertwined with sample size planning, as it represents an alternative approach to traditional statistical power

title: Goal 3: report a CI around the effect size
guidance: Under Goal 3 you run the same analysis as the original, but you also report a confidence interval around your effect size estimate (for example d, a regression coefficient, or R²). Judge success by how precise the estimate is. On its own this does not compare your effect size with the original's, so add Goal 5 or Goal 6 if you need that comparison.
action: Report the replication effect size with its confidence interval.
quote: the author should provide a confidence interval around his or her specified effect size estimate

title: MBESS for effect-size confidence intervals
guidance: The R package MBESS computes confidence intervals for many effect sizes, including the standardized mean difference, regression coefficients, R and R², and standardized contrasts. Bonett (2008, 2009) gives worked calculations of intervals for the SMD across different research designs.
action: Use MBESS (R) or equivalent to compute effect-size CIs.
quote: Packages such as MBESS in R contain user friendly functions for estimating confidence intervals around effect sizes

title: Goal 4: meta-analyse replication with the original
guidance: If you have little reason to think the original study was flawed, you can pool it with your replication in a small meta-analysis to get a more precise estimate. This can be the first step of a continuously cumulating meta-analysis. The authors recommend Bonett's fixed-effect confidence intervals, which cope with heterogeneity, over methods that combine p values. You do not need the original raw data.
action: Compute a pooled effect-size CI combining original and replication (Bonett, 2009).
quote: Bonett (2009) emphasized the benefits of statistically combining a replication attempt with prior studies

title: A nonsignificant replication can strengthen the pooled evidence
guidance: When a nonsignificant replication is combined with the original, the pooled effect can still be significant, and sometimes the evidence against the null is stronger than in the original alone. In the authors' example, the replication alone had d = 0.33 (not significant), but the pooled d of 0.44 had a CI of [0.10, 0.79]. Report the combined estimate before calling the replication a failure.
action: Report the pooled original+replication estimate alongside the standalone result.
quote: a nonsignificant replication attempt may actually lead to stronger evidence against the null hypothesis than the original statistically significant findings

title: Pooling does not fix publication bias
guidance: Combining your replication with the original does not remove publication bias or the upward bias in the original's published effect size. If you suspect the original was inflated or flawed, a pooled estimate carries that bias forward. Say this limitation explicitly when you report Goal 4.
action: Note the original's possible publication bias when interpreting pooled estimates.
quote: this approach does not ameliorate the issue of publication bias or the upward bias often inherent in published effect size estimates

title: Goal 5: CI for the difference in effect sizes
guidance: To claim that your result is clearly inconsistent with the original, compute one confidence interval for the difference between the two effect sizes, for example d(original) − d(replication). Conclude that they differ only if that interval excludes zero. For correlations, Zou's (2007) method gives the interval for the difference between independent correlations.
action: Compute a CI for d_original − d_replication; claim inconsistency only if it excludes 0.
quote: it is necessary to calculate a single confidence interval for the difference between the original and replication effect sizes

title: Do not compare p values or eyeball CI overlap
guidance: Saying the studies differ because one had p < .05 and the other p > .05 is not valid, because the difference between significant and nonsignificant may not itself be significant. Checking whether two confidence intervals overlap is also wrong: intervals that overlap can still come from estimates that differ significantly.
action: Test the original–replication difference directly rather than comparing p values or CI overlap.
quote: two confidence intervals can overlap, but their parameter estimates can still be significantly different from each other

title: A smaller effect is not automatically a nonreplication
guidance: Finding a smaller or nonsignificant effect, even with a bigger sample, does not show that your result differs from the original. In the authors' example, a replication with d = 0.15 against an original d = 0.5 gave a difference CI of [−0.17, 0.87], so no difference could be claimed. Precise comparisons need adequately large samples in both studies.
action: Before claiming nonreplication, check whether the difference CI actually excludes zero.
quote: the width of this confidence interval highlights the difficulty of finding a significant difference between two studies unless both studies have large enough sample sizes

title: Goal 6: equivalence test on the effect-size difference
guidance: To claim your result is clearly consistent with the original, first set bounds, based on theory and earlier work, for a difference in effect sizes you would treat as essentially zero. Then compute a 90% CI for the difference. Claim consistency only if the whole interval lies inside those bounds. Partly overlapping intervals are not conclusive.
action: Preregister bounds for a negligible effect-size difference and test with a 90% CI.
quote: our recommended analysis is an equivalence test on the difference in effect sizes between the original and replication study

title: Not different is not the same as equivalent
guidance: A difference CI that includes zero does not show that your effect matches the original. Even some methods papers make this mistake. In the authors' example, d = 0.48 against 0.5 differed by only 0.02, but the CI of [−0.50, 0.54] did not fit within ±0.15, so equivalence could not be claimed.
action: Only claim 'consistent with the original' after a passed equivalence test.
quote: showing that two studies are not significantly different from each other is not the same as showing that they are indeed equivalent

title: Equivalence with a small original study is hard
guidance: Showing that your effect size matches the original's usually needs very large samples. This is especially true when the original study was small, because its imprecision widens the difference interval however large your own sample is. Check whether Goal 6 is feasible before adopting it.
action: Check feasibility of Goal 6 given the original n before committing to it.
quote: emphasizes the typical requirement of very large sample sizes to have power to establish equivalence, especially when the original study has a small sample size

title: Conceptual replications are harder to interpret
guidance: The article's methods assume a direct replication, and many carry over to conceptual replications. The exceptions include studies with multiple dependent variables. In a conceptual replication, disparate or null results may come from uncontrolled differences in conditions, measures or participants, so record every such difference.
action: List every difference in conditions, measures, and participants from the original.
quote: nonsignificant or disparate findings could be due to a host of uncontrolled factors, such as differences in, conditions, measurement tools, and participants

title: Summary statistics suffice for these analyses
guidance: None of the proposed analyses needs the original raw data, just as a meta-analysis does not. You will need the original's effect size, sample sizes and, for some analyses, the group means and SDs. Goal 5, for example, needs the group variances. Collect these from the paper or from the authors early on.
action: Extract the original's per-group n, means, SDs, and effect size.
quote: access to the raw data is not required for any of our proposed methods

title: One replication rarely settles an effect
guidance: A single replication is usually not enough to accept or reject a published effect with full confidence. Its value grows when it feeds into later meta-analyses of several replications. Present your study as one contribution to that body of evidence.
action: Frame conclusions as one contribution to cumulative evidence, not a final verdict.
quote: a single replication is usually insufficient to accept or refute a published effect with absolute confidence

title: Avoid a black-and-white success/failure verdict
guidance: The authors argue that treating replication as a simple significant-versus-nonsignificant choice has fed the crisis of confidence. Report results for the goals you set, and combine them where useful. For example, give a CI for your effect size (Goal 3) and then compare it with the original (Goal 5).
action: Report results against each preregistered goal rather than a single pass/fail label.
quote: replication should be viewed as a construct that can be amenable to varying purposes

title: Direct replication
guidance: A direct replication reproduces the relevant procedures of the selected study as closely as possible. When it succeeds, it helps rule out false positives and possible experimenter effects. Irvine counts replication as a form of robustness analysis: outcomes are compared across studies to see how well a result holds up when the procedure changes.
action: State which aspects of the original procedure you reproduce as closely as possible.
quote: Successful direct replications help to rule out false positives and possible experimenter effects

title: Conceptual replication
guidance: A conceptual replication keeps the theoretical reasoning of the original study but tests the hypothesis with different procedures or different operationalizations of the variables. When it succeeds, it tells you about how far the underlying theory generalizes.
action: Specify which theoretical claim is retained and which operationalizations change.
quote: Conceptual replications retain the basic theoretical reasoning in the selected study but use different procedures or operationalizations of variables

title: All psychology replications are partly conceptual
guidance: Following Stroebe and Strack and others, Irvine accepts that no psychology replication can use exactly the same causal pathways as the original. Treat 'direct' and 'conceptual' as points on a scale of how causally independent your study is from the original. This also means that a failed 'direct' replication can be dismissed as not a proper replication.
action: Describe your replication by its degree of causal independence from the original.
quote: the causal pathways across replications will never be identical: Because of the subject matter of psychology, all replications are conceptual

title: Aim for psychometric invariance, not identical materials
guidance: Original materials may have been designed for one population or context and may not produce the same psychological phenomenon somewhere else. Following Fabrigar and Wegener, a 'direct' replication should try to recreate the same psychological conditions as the original, adapting the materials where that is needed.
action: Check whether original stimuli will evoke the same psychological state in your population.
quote: to recreate the same psychological conditions as the original study

title: What makes a replication good
guidance: Irvine calls a replication 'good' if it tests the original's core claim convincingly enough that it cannot easily be dismissed. A good replication can either succeed or fail. Only good replications give informative results, and meta-analyses of replications also assume they are good.
action: Identify the original's core claim and explain how your design targets it.
quote: appears to test the core claim from an original study, and does so in a fairly convincing way

title: Anticipate how context changes stimulus effects
guidance: A good direct replication needs background theory about how differences in history, culture, demographics or education might change the way participants respond to the original stimuli. You also need to know how to update the study if they do. Your adaptations do not have to be beyond criticism, but they must be defensible.
action: For each population/context difference, justify whether and how stimuli were adapted.
quote: might affect whether an original set of stimuli will trigger the same psychological response in a new population, and if so, how to update the study

title: Seemingly minor factors get questioned later
guidance: Commentaries on the Many Labs projects questioned many kinds of difference: associations with national symbols, which groups count as out-groups, ambient lab temperature, running several studies in one session, and changes in how stimulus features are rated. Expect such factors to be raised and record them in advance.
action: Document setting details (e.g., lab conditions, study bundling, stimulus norms) versus the original.
quote: ambient lab temperature, participants doing multiple studies in one sitting

title: Conceptual replications demand more theory
guidance: Using new operationalizations requires knowing how else you can intervene on the target phenomenon and measure its effects. Before you choose a conceptual replication, check whether the theory of the phenomenon's causal profile is developed enough to support one.
action: Write out the causal profile (causes/effects) that justifies your new operationalizations.
quote: This demands having a fairly fleshed-out theory of the general causal profile of the target phenomenon: what reliably causes it and what it reliably causes in turn

title: Failed conceptual replications are easy to dismiss
guidance: Because a conceptual replication fills in theoretical detail the original left open, the original authors can reject a failure as not a proper test. Make your theoretical assumptions explicit and defensible, and if possible get agreement on them in advance, to reduce this risk.
action: Make explicit every theoretical assumption your conceptual replication adds.
quote: researchers often have to go out on a theoretical limb to construct a conceptual replication, filling in areas of theoretical detail, that can be easily rejected by the original authors

title: Know how causally independent your replication is
guidance: What your results let you conclude depends on how causally independent your study is from the original. Strong inferences about validity need procedures that are fairly independent. You need to understand the causal profiles of both the measurement procedures and the phenomenon to judge this.
action: Assess and state how causally independent your procedure is from the original.
quote: one also needs to know how causally independent the replication is from the original study

title: Meta-analysing replications assumes they are good
guidance: Several authors recommend combining replications in meta-analyses instead of counting successes and failures. Irvine points out that this only helps if each replication is a good one that really targets the original's core claim. Make that case before pooling.
action: Justify that each study pooled genuinely targets the original core claim.
quote: this suggestion relies on replications being good ones that do genuinely target the core claim from the original study

title: Counting changed design facets misses causal change
guidance: Taxonomies that count how many design facets differ from the original do not measure causal independence. A study that changes every facet may keep the same causal structure, and one change can alter it greatly. Judge each difference by what it does to the causal structure, not by how many there are.
action: For each deviation, note its likely effect on the causal structure, not just its presence.
quote: Assessing causal independence is therefore messier than counting mere changes in experimental design

title: Weak-theory areas make informative replication hard
guidance: The areas of psychology that most need theory development are the ones where informative replications are hardest to run, and in some areas they may not yet be possible. When you choose a target, check whether the background theory is mature enough to design a defensible replication.
action: Assess whether background theory for your target supports a defensible replication.
quote: informative replication studies are much harder to perform. Indeed, in some areas they may currently be impossible

title: Direct replication shows repeatability, not validity
guidance: At most, a successful direct replication shows that the measurement procedure is repeatable. It does not show that the procedure is valid or accurate, or that the theory is true, because a repeatable procedure could be measuring the wrong thing consistently. Regnault's thermometers are the example: repeatability does not imply truth.
action: Limit conclusions from a successful direct replication to repeatability of the procedure.
quote: mere direct replication shows nothing in itself about the accuracy or validity of the measurement procedures or the truth of the underlying theory being tested

title: When direct replication is most useful
guidance: Direct replications add most when you are already fairly confident that the measure validly tests the prediction and the open question is statistical power. Then a well-powered direct replication checks the prediction against more robust data. Direct replications on their own do little to support theory.
action: Check that measure validity is established before relying on a direct replication.
quote: fairly confident that a measurement procedure does validly test a theoretical prediction, but there is a lack of clarity about the statistical power

title: Published measures may not be valid
guidance: In the areas where theory is weakest, there is rarely a set of measures known to be valid. Often it is unclear how valid the measures really are. A replication that repeats an unvalidated measure may just reproduce an artifact of poor operationalization.
action: Review validity evidence for the original measures before reusing them.
quote: there are often questions about just how valid the measurement procedures actually are

title: Even good conceptual replications offer limited payoff
guidance: Philosophers of measurement increasingly agree that conceptual replications are weaker tests than they are usually assumed to be. Procedures often rest on the same theoretical assumptions and so are hardly independent. When procedures interact with the target in similar ways, it is unsurprising that they agree, so do not overstate what your conceptual replication shows about the theory.
action: Temper theoretical claims from a conceptual replication given limited causal independence.
quote: the “causal-independence” requirement on conceptual replications is vague and in any case hardly ever met to a significant degree

title: Set permissible tolerances before comparing results
guidance: Drawing on Meehl, Irvine argues that a meaningful comparison of two results needs a prior expectation, based on background theory, of how close they should be if both measure the same thing. Decide what counts as 'reasonably close' to the original before you compare.
action: Predefine how close your result must be to the original to count as agreement.
quote: comparing two outcomes requires having already established roughly how close you expect them to be if they do in fact both measure the same target variable

title: Use coherent calibration across procedures
guidance: Calibration compares the outcomes of several measurement procedures with each other and with the errors predicted for each one. If they agree once expected errors are accounted for, that supports both the measures and the background theory. If they disagree, revise the procedures or your expectations about them. Basso's poverty-measurement example shows how a known systematic error lets two procedures agree.
action: Compare procedures against predicted error profiles, not just against each other.
quote: systematically comparing the outcomes from a set of measurement procedures with each other, and against theoretical predictions about the kinds of errors or uncertainties associated with each procedure

title: Estimate measurement error in advance
guidance: Beyond knowing the theory, informative replication needs reasonable (not certain) support for the validity and accuracy of your measures. You also need to predict the likely measurement errors across studies before you compare them. For example, if you know a measure underestimates the construct in one group, state that before you interpret any discrepancy.
action: List expected systematic measurement errors across original and replication samples.
quote: support for the general validity and accuracy of the measurement procedures used, and the ability to estimate, in advance, likely measurement errors across different studies

title: The problem of coordination
guidance: Validating a measure needs a theory of the target, and building that theory needs valid measures. Philosophers call this the problem of coordination. It is why measurement and theory have to develop together, step by step, rather than one waiting for the other.
action: Note where your measure's validity depends on theory that is itself unsettled.
quote: you cannot know whether you have a good way of “getting at” something unless you have a good idea what it is

title: Progress is iterative: enrichment and self-correction
guidance: In current philosophy of science, theory and experiment improve together in small local steps. Following Chang, progress comes through enrichment (more precision and scope) and self-correction (more accurate predictions and measurements). Either way it builds on existing theory and existing procedures.
action: Position your replication as a step that builds on existing theory and procedures.
quote: progress is made possible only by building on existing theoretical knowledge and existing experimental procedures—both are required

title: One round of replication cannot settle an effect
guidance: Irvine calls two expectations unrealistic in any science: that good replications can be run without well-developed theory, and that one round of replication can confirm or disconfirm an effect. Do not present your single study as the final word on whether the effect exists.
action: Avoid claiming your single replication confirms or disconfirms the effect.
quote: a single round of replication studies should be able to confirm or disconfirm the existence of an effect. These expectations are wholly unrealistic

title: Frame replication attempts as exploratory studies
guidance: Where theory is thin, and often even where it is not, Irvine suggests treating replication attempts as exploratory studies that support stages of theory development. That means stating which causal factors you assume matter, testing the claim again, and using any discrepancies to refine theory or experimental controls.
action: State the exploratory, theory-building role of your replication in your aims.
quote: are much better seen as exploratory studies that support different stages of theory development concerning a target phenomenon

title: Build theory to explain unexpected results
guidance: When your results differ from the prediction, develop theory to explain the difference and use it to update the overall theory or improve experimental controls. Then test again. This can mean making claims more precise or mapping the conditions under which the effect occurs.
action: Propose explicit, testable explanations for any discrepancy with the original.
quote: The results are often different from what was predicted, at which point more theory is constructed to explain the differences

title: Test the underlying assumptions (self-correction)
guidance: Sometimes you need to step back from the main theory and test the assumptions under it, or under the measurement procedure. Identify those assumptions systematically, test whether they hold, and update them if they do not. This is a legitimate follow-up to a replication.
action: List key auxiliary assumptions and suggest how each could be tested.
quote: Self-correction can involve systematically identifying the underlying assumptions of a theory or measurement procedure, testing and exploring them to see whether they are warranted

title: Follow the observe-hypothesize-test model
guidance: After a null replication (Many Labs 3), Luttrell et al. identified factors that might explain it and manipulated them experimentally. Ebersole et al. then replicated that follow-up across nine sites. Treat the difference between original and replication as something to study, not something to argue away.
action: Design a follow-up that manipulates the factors hypothesised to explain the discrepancy.
quote: explicitly manipulated these factors experimentally to investigate whether they were indeed the cause of the null result

title: Exploratory framing invites engagement
guidance: If a replication is treated as a single round whose success or failure simply stands, nobody has a reason to follow it up. Presenting it as the exploratory study it often is invites others to engage with it and explore further. Write your discussion so that it opens questions for follow-up work.
action: End your report with concrete open questions and next studies.
quote: Treating replication attempts as exploratory studies, which is often what they actually are, shifts this treatment: Exploratory studies invite engagement and further exploration

title: Valid scores are a prerequisite for valid conclusions
guidance: Construct validation is the process of gathering evidence that a score really means what you claim it means (e.g., that higher scores reflect more motivation). If the numbers in a study do not reflect the intended construct, the study's conclusions are not valid either, and this applies equally to your replication.
action: Write down, for each key variable, what construct its score is claimed to represent.
quote: If the numbers used in a study are not valid (e.g., the motivation scores do not reflect levels of motivation) then the conclusions of that study are also not valid.

title: Validity belongs to score interpretations, not instruments
guidance: Validity is not a yes/no property of a questionnaire; it is a judgment about how scores are interpreted, based on accumulating evidence. Because the same instrument can behave differently in a new context or population, evidence gathered in the original study does not automatically carry over to your replication sample.
action: Plan to collect validity evidence for scores in your own replication context.
quote: validity is not a binary property of an instrument, but instead a judgment made about the score interpretation based on a body of accumulating evidence

title: Three phases of validity evidence
guidance: Validity evidence comes in phases: substantive (content and response processes, e.g., expert item review, think-aloud), structural (item, factor and reliability analyses, e.g., CFA plus reliability), and external (relations to other variables, e.g., MTMM, prediction). Since replications usually test relationships between constructs, substantive and structural evidence should be in place first.
action: Check which substantive, structural and external evidence exists for each primary measure.
quote: Using scores to understand the downstream relationships between constructs is often the goal of a replication study, thus substantive and structural validity evidence are a pre-requisite.

title: Good statistics cannot rescue poor measurement
guidance: A lack of construct validity cannot be fixed by better statistical practice such as high power or preregistered analyses. Just as a replication of a study with a failed manipulation is not meaningful, a replication whose measures lack validity evidence says little, however rigorous its statistics.
action: Give measurement validity the same planning attention as power and analysis.
quote: If a researcher uses scale scores with limited validity evidence, this lack of construct validity cannot be ameliorated through improving statistical practices.

title: Cronbach's alpha is not validity evidence
guidance: Many researchers rely on alpha as the only support for a score, but reliability shows consistency, not meaning: scores can be reliable yet not represent the intended construct. Alpha is also only interpretable under a single-factor model with equal loadings, so do not treat a high alpha as sufficient validation.
action: Do not report alpha as your sole evidence that a measure is valid.
quote: Reliability coefficients are not evidence of validity: scores can be reliable (i.e., consistent) but not convey the meaning intended

title: Alpha assumes a single factor with equal loadings
guidance: The most commonly reported psychometric statistic, alpha, rests on strong assumptions about scale structure. Before interpreting alpha in your replication sample, check whether a unidimensional structure is plausible, and choose a more appropriate reliability estimate if it is not.
action: Check dimensionality before reporting alpha; use a fitting reliability coefficient otherwise.
quote: a single factor model with equal loadings is necessary for the valid interpretation of α reliability coefficients, which are the most common psychometric information reported.

title: Expect missing measurement details in the original
guidance: In the RPP, many original scales lacked basic information: number of items (8%), response format (6%), and, for multi-item scales, how they were scored (51%). Some replicators found item wording misreported or could not match scoring even after obtaining materials and with author cooperation, so verify these details explicitly.
action: Confirm item wording, number of items, response format, and scoring rule for every measure.
quote: number of items not reported (8%), response format not reported (6%), and how the scale was scored not reported (scales with more than 1-item, 51%).

title: Primary measures often lack validity evidence
guidance: Most RPP scales (71%) had no citation to published validity evidence, and 20% of multi-item primary measures came with no validity or reliability information at all, suggesting many were created on the fly. Replicating such a study means inheriting that lack of evidence unless you add your own.
action: Search for published validation studies for each primary measure you will use.
quote: Of all the scales used in the reproducibility project, 71% had no citation to published validity evidence in the original study.

title: Screen candidate studies for validity evidence
guidance: Some original effects rest on such weak foundations that replicating them wastes resources. Select studies for direct replication that offer a severe test of the hypothesis, based on a review of construct, statistical, internal and external validity; weak substantive or structural evidence in the original will carry over into your replication.
action: Review the original's construct validity evidence before committing to replicate it.
quote: scientists should only select studies for direct replication that provide a severe test of the hypothesis (Mayo, 2019) via a thorough review of the validity evidence

title: Justify selection by strength of original evidence
guidance: Large projects often picked studies by journal, period, novelty or impact. The authors recommend balancing those criteria with the strength of the original evidence, so that the replication yields results with fewer threats to validity and a better return on the effort invested.
action: Include the strength of original validity evidence in your target-study justification.
quote: a balanced approach that justifies selection based on the strength of the original evidence alongside those other considerations would result in replication studies that are a good return on investment

title: Build minimum validity checks into the replication
guidance: If the original provides little validity evidence and you still replicate it, gather evidence yourself. At a minimum: review items or stimuli for face and content validity, check the assumed scoring structure (e.g., component or factor analysis), and report an appropriate reliability estimate. Treat these like a manipulation check or sample size plan.
action: Plan an item review, a structure check, and an appropriate reliability estimate.
quote: checks on assumed scoring structure when applicable (e.g., using a component or factor analysis), and reporting of an appropriate measure of reliability.

title: Report the strength of validity evidence transparently
guidance: Some construct validity evidence is better than none. Transparently reporting how strong or weak the evidence is for your measures in the replication sample is an important first step toward more valid replication research.
action: Report the validity and reliability evidence obtained in your replication sample.
quote: Some construct validity evidence is more than none, and transparent reporting of the strength of the evidence in a replication study is an important first step

title: Improving measures turns direct into conceptual replication
guidance: Instead of reusing a weak measure, you can use a different or redeveloped instrument. This rules out a direct replication, but gives a stronger, different test of the original claim while still assessing generalizability. There is limited value in a study whose results remain open to alternative explanations due to poor construct validity.
action: Decide whether to keep original measures (direct) or improve them (approximate), and justify it.
quote: Another option is to improve upon the measures (e.g., use different or redeveloped instruments), which would preclude a direct replication.

title: Acknowledge weak construct validity in interpretation
guidance: Whether your replication is direct or approximate, weigh all validity evidence when interpreting the result. If construct validity evidence is weak, state this explicitly as a threat to validity, just as you would a confound, in the final interpretation of the replication effect.
action: State explicitly any weak construct validity evidence when interpreting the replication result.
quote: If construct validity evidence is weak, like other threats to validity (e.g., confounds), that should be explicitly acknowledged in the final interpretation of the replication effect.

title: Same scale, same protocol, different measurement
guidance: Measurement differences arise not only from changed item wording, presentation or response options, but also when the same scale and protocol are used. Psychometric analyses in the replication sample may show that you are not measuring the same construct as the original, which undermines comparing scores across studies.
action: Compare your sample's psychometric results with the original's, even for unchanged scales.
quote: Changes to the item wording, presentation, and response options introduces measurement differences that may interfere with the comparison of the scores from original to replication study.

title: Lower reliability and item removal
guidance: In one RPP replication, most scales had lower reliability than in the original, and replicators removed items to raise alpha. Beyond the reliability gap, dropping items can reduce content validity, leaving the replication with weaker content evidence than the original. Document any such changes and their consequences.
action: Document reliability differences and any item removal, noting possible loss of content validity.
quote: item removal could decrease the content validity of the instrument, causing the replication study to have less evidence of content than the original.

title: Check item intercorrelations before averaging
guidance: Averaging items into a composite assumes they share a common construct. In one RPP case, two items correlated r = .63 originally but only r = .17 in the replication; the replicator followed the original protocol but also analysed each item separately. Check whether your data still justify the original aggregation.
action: Check item intercorrelations in your data before forming composites; report item-level analyses if weak.
quote: A large correlation justifies the averaging of responses of the two items because their shared variation could be attributed to a common construct

title: When factor structure does not replicate
guidance: In one RPP replication, an exploratory factor analysis found two factors where the original used three subscales; the replicator scored per the original protocol, producing scores unsupported by the data. There is a tension between scoring as in the original and scoring as your data support, so plan in advance how you will handle it.
action: Pre-specify how you will score scales if the original factor structure is not supported.
quote: There is a tension between using the scales in the same way as the original versus using the scales supported by the factor analysis results

title: Translated scales need validation
guidance: Forty RPP scales were translated, and only 20% used an existing translation with validity evidence. Even careful translation with multiple translators and back-translation is not enough: scores from translated scales need validation to confirm they capture the construct comparably. Validated translations of some scales (e.g., PANAS) have shown non-equivalence.
action: Use a validated translation if available; otherwise plan to validate your translated scores.
quote: scores from translated scales require validation after the initial translation to confirm that translated items are capturing the construct in a comparable way.

title: Comparability requires measurement equivalence
guidance: A replication assumes constructs are the same and measures equivalent across studies. Scores are equivalent when their properties do not differ across time, groups or settings. Replications happen later, in different places and often languages, all of which can cause non-equivalence, visible as different factor structures or reliabilities.
action: List time, setting, population, and language differences that might threaten measurement equivalence.
quote: Measurement equivalence is necessary for results from the original and replication studies to be comparable.

title: Expect non-equivalence in translated instruments
guidance: Replicators should anticipate that translated instruments will not function identically; international testing often finds many differentially functioning items. In Many Labs 2, translated instruments showed lower reliability on average than those administered in the original language.
action: Budget time and analyses for testing equivalence of any translated instrument.
quote: This challenge is well documented in international achievement testing and studies often report a substantial number of non-equivalent items

title: Methods for evaluating measurement equivalence
guidance: Established psychometric methods can be brought into replication work: item response theory or confirmatory factor analysis to detect differential item functioning, and think-aloud protocols to check that participants understand items as intended or that translations are accurate. Equivalence is tested through successively more restrictive models.
action: Plan a CFA/IRT invariance or DIF test comparing original-language and replication data where possible.
quote: Examples include using item response theory or confirmatory factor analysis to identify differential item functioning, in addition to think a-loud protocols

title: Don't interpret the effect if measures failed
guidance: If evidence shows that foundational aspects (like measurement) are not comparable between original and replication, interpreting the downstream hypothesis test does not make sense, just as you would not test group differences after a failed manipulation. Measurement differences also offer an explanation for replication failure beyond a Type I error in the original.
action: Before interpreting the effect, confirm measurement comparability; discuss non-equivalence as an explanation.
quote: When evidence points to a failure to achieve comparable foundational aspects between the original and replication study, it is not sensible to interpret the downstream test

title: Replicability is not validity
guidance: Construct validity is necessary but not sufficient for replication: studies with valid measures may still fail to replicate if the original was a Type I error, and some invalid studies do replicate. When reporting, distinguish how consistent a finding is from how meaningful it is.
action: In your discussion, address both consistency of the effect and validity of its measures.
quote: Replicability tells us how consistent a finding is; it does not tell us if the finding is valid.

title: Equivalence can be partial, not all-or-nothing
guidance: Measurement equivalence is not a binary property; some items can be equivalent while others are not. There are also scoring approaches that account for non-equivalence in downstream analyses. The authors note that clear guidelines for replicators do not yet exist, so justify your chosen approach.
action: If full invariance fails, examine item-level (partial) equivalence and justify your scoring approach.
quote: Measurement equivalence is not a binary property of an instrument (Horn & McArdle, 1992) and some items can be equivalent while others are not

title: Choose among candidates under resource limits
guidance: Replicators almost never have the time or money to replicate everything they find interesting, so target selection is a choice among a set of candidate claims. Treat it as an explicit decision: compare several candidate claims rather than committing to the first study that comes to mind.
action: List your candidate claims and compare them before committing to one target.
quote: replicating researchers are constrained by resources, and will almost always have to choose one replication effort to focus on from a set of potential candidates

title: Replication value: value times uncertainty
guidance: Isager et al. define a claim's replication value as the most expected utility a replication could add. It depends on two things: how valuable it would be to know for certain whether the claim is true, and how uncertain the current evidence leaves us. A candidate scores high only when both are substantial.
action: Rate each candidate claim separately on value and on current uncertainty.
quote: is a function of (a) the value of being certain about the claim, and (b) uncertainty about the claim based on current evidence

title: Four factors in deciding what to replicate
guidance: A review of justifications given in published replications and of earlier proposals points to four recurring considerations: the value of the research topic, uncertainty about the current state of knowledge, the quality of the proposed replication (its ability to reduce that uncertainty), and the costs and feasibility of running it. Your target worksheet should address all four rather than just one.
action: Score each candidate on value, uncertainty, replication quality, and cost/feasibility.
quote: four factors when deciding what would be worth replicating: (a)

title: Value: importance of knowing the claim's truth
guidance: In the model, value is how important it is to gain certain knowledge about whether the claim is true or false. It typically reflects the claim's impact, for instance its theoretical implications, its potential for application, or the pure goal of knowing. Articulate for whom (researchers, practitioners, the public) the answer matters.
action: Write one sentence on why knowing whether this claim is true matters, and to whom.
quote: The value of a claim is deﬁned as the importance of gaining

title: Uncertainty: why current evidence is inconclusive
guidance: Uncertainty before replication reflects how unsure we are that the claim is true given existing knowledge (0 = certain, 1 = completely uncertain). Sources include a sparse or ambiguous evidence base, imprecise effect estimates, low validity of existing designs, and publication bias or other factors inflating false positives. Name the specific sources that apply to your candidate.
action: Document the concrete sources of uncertainty (sparse evidence, imprecision, weak designs, bias) for each candidate.
quote: claim. For example, the current evidence base may be sparse or

title: Prioritise valuable claims we are unsure about
guidance: Because replication value multiplies value by uncertainty, it is highest for important claims whose truth is still genuinely in doubt. Conversely, it is low for uncertain claims nobody needs to know about and for important claims that are already well established.
action: Flag candidates that are high on both value and uncertainty as priority targets.
quote: valuable claims that we are very uncertain about before replication.

title: Don't replicate what is already settled
guidance: A replication adds little if the claim is either not worth knowing or already firmly established; the authors illustrate this with repeated replications of a classroom-staple effect. Before investing effort, check whether prior replications already leave little uncertainty about your candidate claim.
action: Search for existing replications of each candidate and note how settled the claim already is.
quote: Conversely, replication value will be low for highly uncertain claims

title: Weigh expected gain against cost
guidance: When candidates have similar replication value, prefer the one that delivers the most knowledge per unit of resources, the idea of marginal utility per dollar. Lower cost, all else equal, means a higher gain per resource spent, so cost belongs on your worksheet next to value and uncertainty.
action: Estimate the cost of replicating each candidate and compare knowledge gained per unit of cost.
quote: the largest increase in scientiﬁc knowledge per dollar spent on the

title: Count non-monetary costs too
guidance: Costs are not just money: the expertise you would need to acquire and the working hours required also count. For a PhD student, time, skills to learn, and access to equipment or populations are often the binding constraints.
action: List money, time, expertise, and access requirements for each candidate replication.
quote: nonmonetary resources such as the amount of expertise we need to

title: Some targets are simply infeasible
guidance: Occasionally a replication's costs are so high that it cannot be done at all, for example when the required population would take decades or more money than is available to reach. Rule such candidates out early instead of discovering infeasibility mid-project.
action: Drop any candidate whose required population, data, or budget is out of reach.
quote: Sometimes the costs of a replication study are so high that it is

title: Replication quality: ability to reduce uncertainty
guidance: In this model, a replication's quality is simply how much it can reduce uncertainty about the claim. A high-quality replication shrinks uncertainty more than a low-quality one, so the design you can realistically run is part of the target decision.
action: Judge how much your feasible design would actually reduce uncertainty about each candidate claim.
quote: in our model, simply deﬁned as the ability of the replication study

title: Spend resources to raise replication quality
guidance: When a replication is feasible, extra resources can usually buy a bigger reduction in uncertainty, for example by recruiting more participants to increase statistical power or by doing more pilot work to validate measures and run manipulation checks. Budget for these quality improvements explicitly.
action: Allocate budget for larger samples and pilot work validating measures and manipulations.
quote: be done for instance by recruiting more participants to increase

title: A flawed original design limits what replication can teach
guidance: A claim can be valuable and uncertain yet still be a poor target: if the uncertainty stems mainly from a low-quality original design that the replication would repeat, replicating it will barely reduce uncertainty. Check that the original design is good enough for a repetition of it to be informative.
action: Assess whether the original design is sound enough that repeating it would be informative.
quote: to consider whether the original study design is of sufﬁcient qual-

title: Indicators for operationalising value
guidance: Isager et al. suggest possible quantitative indicators of a claim's value, such as citation counts, Altmetric Attention scores, journal impact indicators, best-paper awards, citation in textbooks, clinical guidelines or policy, and reviewer ratings of importance. These are only proxies: they are valid only to the extent that valuable claims tend to be cited more, and their validity differs across fields (field-weighted citations are often preferable). Choose indicators suited to your field and record them for every candidate.
action: Record comparable value indicators (e.g., citations, policy/textbook uptake, awards) for every candidate.
quote: The scientiﬁc and societal impact of a claim are widely consid-

title: Impact metrics are only proxies for value
guidance: Citation counts or Altmetric scores do not make a claim valuable; they are valid only insofar as valuable claims tend to be cited more. Where possible, also judge value directly, such as the claim's importance for theory or its potential to reduce harm through policy.
action: Supplement citation-based indicators with a direct judgement of theoretical or practical importance.
quote: Note that impact metrics are not part of the value construct as such.

title: Indicators for operationalising uncertainty
guidance: Possible quantitative indicators of pre-replication uncertainty include sample size, Bayesian posteriors or Bayes factors, number of prior replications, prediction-market ratings, variance of effect estimates, statistical power of existing studies, prevalence of reporting errors, and bias estimates. Record several for each candidate.
action: Record uncertainty indicators (sample size, power, prior replications, reporting errors) for every candidate.
quote: include sample size (Fraley & Vazire, 2014), Bayesian posterior

title: Combine value and uncertainty multiplicatively
guidance: Following decision theory, the value and uncertainty estimates should be multiplied, not added, to obtain replication value. Indicators may first need transforming so they behave like the model's terms; for example, a replication probability must be converted so that maximal doubt (around .5) yields maximal uncertainty.
action: Compute each candidate's replication value as (value score) x (uncertainty score) after rescaling both.
quote: theory, the two terms should be multiplied (see the structural equa-

title: Transform indicators to fit the model
guidance: Raw indicators rarely map directly onto value or uncertainty. The authors' hypothetical example transforms a prediction-market probability so that uncertainty is highest when the market is at .5 and lowest when it is at 0 or 1. Check that each indicator you use increases in the intended direction.
action: Check and, if needed, transform each indicator so higher scores mean more value or uncertainty.
quote: Indicators might often need to be transformed to behave in

title: Value judgements depend on who evaluates
guidance: Value is subjective, so a claim's replication value depends on the evaluator and context; funders, journals, and researchers may legitimately weight things differently. State whose perspective (e.g., your field, a target journal, practitioners) your value ratings reflect.
action: State whose perspective your value ratings represent.
quote: variables. In addition, because value is subjective, the value of a

title: Use a two-stage quantitative-then-qualitative screen
guidance: Quantitative scores are cheap but miss things such as suspected questionable research practices or a finding's importance for theory. The authors expect it to be most efficient to use quantitative replication-value estimates to shortlist promising candidates, then evaluate the shortlist qualitatively before choosing.
action: Shortlist candidates by quantitative score, then qualitatively review the top few before deciding.
quote: Finally, we should note that it is wise to combine quantitative

title: Add qualitative judgements numbers can't capture
guidance: Some determinants of value and uncertainty resist quantification, such as concerns about questionable research practices in the original study or the theoretical importance of a particular observation. Record these as qualitative notes alongside your scores so they inform the final choice.
action: Add qualitative notes on QRP concerns and theoretical importance for each shortlisted candidate.
quote: cannot easily be quantiﬁed, such as concerns about questionable

title: Make your selection procedure transparent
guidance: A clearly defined, standardised selection procedure can be applied consistently to all candidates and shows exactly how the choice was made, which makes disagreements easy to locate and resolve. Even an informal version helps you articulate why you are replicating this particular study.
action: Write down your selection criteria and scoring rules before ranking candidates.
quote: transparent about how studies will be selected. They can hence be

title: Tailor indicators to your field
guidance: Researchers may reasonably disagree about which variables best capture value and uncertainty, and relevance varies across fields; for instance, citation impact is a better value proxy in some fields than others, and field-weighted citation counts are usually preferable to raw counts. Justify your indicator choices for your field.
action: Justify why your chosen indicators are valid for your research field.
quote: identify which factors are most relevant given a particular research

title: Replication value supports ranking, not ratios
guidance: Because replication value assumes all uncertainty could be removed, it overestimates the actual gain; it is useful for ranking candidates, not for saying one is twice as worth replicating as another. Use your scores to order candidates, not to make interval-scale claims.
action: Use replication-value scores only to rank candidates, not to claim precise magnitudes.
quote: cannot use replication value to evaluate whether one study is twice as

title: Your candidate set limits your choice
guidance: Replication value only compares the candidates you considered; it cannot tell you whether replication beats a novel study, nor whether your candidate set is any good. If all candidates are low-value claims, it is better to assemble a new set than to pick the best of a weak list.
action: Check that your candidate list includes genuinely important claims in your field before ranking.
quote: licate but it does not necessarily help us select a good set of studies

title: Don't game replication value indicators
guidance: Quantitative replication-value estimates can be gamed, for example by inflating a target paper's Altmetric score to meet a funder's threshold, which undermines their validity much as p-hacking undermines p-values. Report your indicators honestly and as found.
action: Record indicator values as found, with retrieval date, without inflating them.
quote: tative estimates of replication value could be “gamed” to achieve

title: Utility-based selection doesn't fit every aim
guidance: The decision model assumes your goal is to maximise the utility of the knowledge gained. If instead your aim is to estimate a field's overall replication rate, studies must be sampled at random, and selecting by replication value would introduce selection bias. Match your selection strategy to your aim.
action: Confirm your replication aim fits value-based target selection rather than random sampling.
quote: tion value prevents random sampling of studies and introduces

title: Use the model to articulate your rationale
guidance: Thinking explicitly about value, uncertainty, replication quality, and cost helps you state clearly why you are replicating a study, even if your selection is less formal than the full model. Use the worksheet output to write your target justification.
action: Write a short target justification covering value, uncertainty, replication quality, and cost.
quote: should also help individual researchers to more clearly formulate

title: Reproducibility vs replication
guidance: Obenauer, following Köhler and Cortina, distinguishes reproducibility (reanalysing an existing dataset) from replication (re-examining relationships with a different dataset). Knowing which you are doing shapes your whole design and how you describe the study.
action: State whether your study reanalyses existing data (reproducibility) or collects new data (replication).
quote: Reproducibility refers to reanalyzing a dataset, whereas replication refers to the reexamination of relationships through the use of a different dataset

title: Literal vs constructive replication
guidance: Literal replication or reproducibility follows the target study's procedures as closely as possible. Constructive replication or reproducibility follows some procedures but makes strategic modifications to test the phenomenon more robustly or strengthen insights.
action: Classify your planned study as literal or constructive, and list any strategic modifications.
quote: refer to studies in which researchers follow some procedures from the target study, but make strategic modiﬁcations

title: Identify your purpose before your target
guidance: Decide why you are replicating before choosing what to replicate; the purpose guides target selection and how you frame the work for your audience. Possible purposes include updating a theory after a relevant event, testing an established theory with stronger methods, probing boundary conditions, advancing a methodological precedent, doctoral training, or meeting a special-issue call.
action: Write down your replication purpose(s) before shortlisting target studies.
quote: Before choosing a replication target, it is important to identify the purpose of your replication study.

title: Include a theoretical purpose
guidance: Management reviewers place heavy weight on theoretical contribution, so even pragmatically motivated replications should carry a theoretical purpose. Obenauer describes adding a purpose of updating a theory after demographic change, which became the manuscript's main framing.
action: Articulate the theoretical purpose your replication serves, alongside any pragmatic motives.
quote: researchers pursuing replication should incorporate a theoretical purpose into their work as well.

title: Choose a purpose you care about
guidance: Publishing replications can be arduous and frustrating because authors, reviewers, and editors often lack a shared understanding of replication. Genuine passion for the purpose helps you persevere through that process.
action: Check that you are genuinely motivated by the purpose you identified.
quote: Having a passion for the research’s purpose helps authors persevere through these types of challenges.

title: Name one clearly identified target study
guidance: Editors and reviewers expect a clearly cited original study; almost all published management replications Obenauer reviewed had a single identified target. Even when your work relates to several studies, name a focal target so readers know the reference point.
action: Identify and cite one focal target study as the reference point for your replication.
quote: Doing so clariﬁes for the reader what they should be using as a referent point.

title: Screen targets for fit with your purpose
guidance: Start the search by identifying studies aligned with your purposes, for example relevance to a special issue's theory, a clearly reported design with features you can vary, or publication before a relevant societal change. Use your purposes as explicit selection criteria.
action: Turn each of your purposes into a selection criterion and screen candidate studies against them.
quote: I recommend beginning by attempting to identify studies that are aligned with your identiﬁed purposes.

title: Reviewers care about the target's impact
guidance: Reviewers, editors, and readers judge a replication partly by the impact of the original; replicating a low-impact publication will likely be seen as adding little. In Obenauer's sample, most published management replication targets had at least 200 citations and only three had fewer than 50.
action: Record the target's citation count and other impact indicators at the time of selection.
quote: the value of replicating a low-impact publication is likely to be perceived as minimal.

title: Find other impact signals for less-cited targets
guidance: If a candidate is not well cited, look for other evidence of impact, such as wide discussion in academia and the press, awards, download counts, or relevance to a journal's call. Obenauer justified a 58-citation target partly because it had won an award.
action: For less-cited targets, document alternative impact evidence (awards, downloads, media, calls).
quote: When considering a replication target that is not well-cited, there should be other important indicators of impact.

title: Build a candidate-target spreadsheet
guidance: Obenauer and Rezaei tabulated every article in the target journal, sorted by downloads, then reviewed the top ten abstracts for fit with their expertise, importance of theoretical contribution, potential replicability, and presence of a relevant post-publication event justifying an update. Use a similar table to compare candidates systematically.
action: Build a spreadsheet of candidate studies with impact metrics and screening-criteria columns.
quote: We started by building a spreadsheet with data on every article in the journal

title: Weigh the publication risk of unusual targets
guidance: Targeting a little-cited paper or a conference proceeding can be justified, for example by the importance of the research question, but it is risky: if the intended journal rejects it, alternative outlets may be limited. Consider this risk explicitly before finalising your target.
action: Note the publication risks of your target choice and your fallback outlets.
quote: Researchers should carefully consider such risks when selecting replication targets.

title: Run an outcome thought experiment
guidance: After preliminary target selection, list every combination of replicated and non-replicated findings (e.g., three hypotheses give eight combinations) and state the contribution each would make. If you cannot identify a contribution for every combination, reconsider whether the target is appropriate.
action: List every combination of replication outcomes and write the contribution each would make.
quote: the researcher should attempt to identify the potential contribution for each combination of outcomes.

title: Tie hypotheses to your success definition
guidance: What counts as successful replication can become a point of dispute in review if not defined in advance. Define the hypotheses you will test and link each to your definition of success; in literal replications you can restate the original hypotheses, and new variables need motivated new hypotheses.
action: Write each hypothesis and specify in advance what result counts as successful replication.
quote: clearly deﬁne the hypotheses that you will be testing and connect them to your deﬁnition of successful replication.

title: Research questions make success harder to define
guidance: You can frame a replication around research questions instead of hypotheses, but this can make it harder to say whether the replication succeeded. If you use research questions, be especially explicit about success criteria.
action: If using research questions instead of hypotheses, write explicit success criteria for each.
quote: though this method can make deﬁning successful replication more difﬁcult.

title: Start with a literal replication before modifying
guidance: Management reviewers tend to prefer constructive replications, but these are stronger when preceded by a literal replication. Establishing that you can recover the original relationships lets you attribute later deviations to your strategic modifications rather than to idiosyncratic effects.
action: Plan a literal replication (or reproduction) before any constructive modifications.
quote: constructive replication studies can be strengthened by starting with a literal replication study.

title: Reproduce the original with the same data first
guidance: In a constructive reproducibility study, Obenauer first reproduced the original results using the original data and methods before adding new variables. Without this step, deviations could not reasonably be attributed to the new variables.
action: Reproduce the original results with the original data before introducing new variables.
