quote: I had to demonstrate that I could reproduce the results of the original study through literal reproduction using the same data.

title: Repeat a literal replication that fails
guidance: When their literal replications produced results different from the original, Obenauer and Kalsher repeated one to reduce the chance the deviation was idiosyncratic, and then compared constructive to literal results. Consider repetition before concluding that a finding did not replicate.
action: If a literal replication diverges, consider repeating it before drawing conclusions.
quote: we then repeated one of the literal replications to reduce the likelihood that deviations in ﬁndings were idiosyncratic.

title: Decide deliberately which studies to replicate
guidance: When a target paper reports several studies, there is no single right choice: replicating all of them limits room for constructive extensions, while replicating only one or two may miss relationships spanning studies. Make the choice deliberately and explain how it strengthens your contribution.
action: Decide which studies in the target paper you will replicate and justify the choice.
quote: researchers should be deliberate in this decision and clearly communicate how their strategic choice enhances their contribution

title: Run an independent power analysis
guidance: Don't simply copy the original sample size: the original may have been underpowered, and replication effects are often smaller, requiring larger samples. Justify your sample with your own power analysis, or reviewers may attribute a failure to replicate to weak design.
action: Run your own power analysis and justify the sample size instead of copying the original.
quote: Replication researchers should conduct independent power analyses and use these to justify sample sizes.

title: Plan for contingencies in advance
guidance: Pretest failures, attention and manipulation checks, and response rates matter even more in replication because they can determine whether you report success. Specify ahead of time what you will do if, for example, a manipulation pretest fails or a minimum sample size is not reached.
action: Pre-specify responses to failed pretests, failed manipulation checks, and missed minimum sample sizes.
quote: What we had not done, however, was specify what we would do if our minimum sample size was not met.

title: Pre-decide exclusions for failed manipulation checks
guidance: In Obenauer and Kalsher's replication, whether participants failing manipulation checks were excluded changed whether the finding replicated, and this was not in their analysis plan. They reported both analyses, but the issue drew scrutiny in review; decide exclusion rules beforehand.
action: Specify in your analysis plan how participants failing manipulation or attention checks are handled.
quote: A decision that we were faced with, however, was what to do with participants who failed manipulation checks.

title: Consider a registered report
guidance: In a registered report, peer review takes place before data collection. Obenauer's team benefited because their response to a failed manipulation pretest had already been defined and accepted by reviewers, and a minimum sample size had been pre-approved.
action: Consider submitting your replication as a registered report before collecting data.
quote: our work had been submitted as a registered report, a process in which peer review also occurs prior to data collection

title: Preregister to force a priori decisions
guidance: Preregistration logs hypotheses and plans for design and analysis in a discoverable repository, and platforms such as OSF push you to decide methodological choices in advance. It need not restrict you: changes requested in peer review can be added as a transparent, explained update.
action: Preregister hypotheses, design, and analysis plan on a platform such as OSF.
quote: it forces researchers to address speciﬁc methodological choices, such as those described above, a priori.

title: Explain why replication is needed at all
guidance: Reviewers often ask why replication is necessary, so include one or two introductory paragraphs making the general case. Obenauer does this even when responding to a replication call, because reviewers may have little experience with replication.
action: Draft one or two introduction paragraphs on why replication matters for robust science.
quote: I began including one to two paragraphs in my introduction that made this case to reviewers.

title: Frame replication as building, not attacking
guidance: Motivate replication as contributing to cumulative science rather than as correcting sampling error or questionable practices in the original. Arguments about flaws are falsifiable and can be rebutted, while a constructive framing invites reviewers to be partners in building better science.
action: Check that your motivation doesn't rely on alleging errors or QRPs in the original study.
quote: The need for replication has been clearly positioned as not attacking prior research.

title: Motivate the target by its importance
guidance: Explain why the specific target deserves replication by stressing its importance (citations, theoretical influence, policy relevance) and what your replication adds, instead of dwelling on perceived problems. Obenauer reports that a critique-style framing drew less receptive reviews than framing as an extension.
action: Write a target rationale emphasising the study's impact and your added contribution.
quote: focusing on establishing the importance of the target study along with how the current replication will contribute to the literature

title: Keep criticism of the original to a minimum
guidance: Critiquing the original's methods is sometimes necessary, for example when small samples may explain null findings, but it should be limited. A replication that has merit even if the original has no flaws tends to be seen as a stronger contribution.
action: Make sure your contribution holds even if the original study had no methodological flaws.
quote: If one can argue that a replication has merit in the absence of methodological ﬂaws in the target study, its contribution will likely be perceived as stronger.

title: Define your replication type explicitly
guidance: Reviewers ask what type of replication you did, so define your replication methodology as you would a statistical analysis. Terminology varies widely across journals, which makes an explicit definition essential.
action: State the type of replication you conduct, with a citation to its definition.
quote: just as we would deﬁne a statistical analysis, researchers should deﬁne their replication methodology.

title: Map your terminology onto the journal's
guidance: Adopt one established replication vocabulary for consistency across your work, but also use the target journal's terms, for example by naming both (e.g., 'narrow replication, also referred to as literal reproducibility'). Journals such as SMJ, JOMSR, Leadership Quarterly and JGM use different labels for the same design.
action: Check the target journal's replication terminology and cross-reference it to your own.
quote: you must also recognize the standard of the journal you are targeting and adhere to that standard.

title: Describe methods in full detail
guidance: Reviewers of replications resist being told to consult the original for methods; they care more about methodological detail than usual and know the target less well than you. Report key details in the manuscript and put the rest in online appendices or an OSF project.
action: Describe all methods in the manuscript or an appendix/OSF project rather than referring to the original.
quote: because methodological details are critical to replication design, reviewers may be more interested in these details than they typically are.

title: Share extensive replication details on OSF
guidance: Showing how faithfully you followed the original methods takes a lot of detail that may bore theory-focused readers. Obenauer puts the extensive details of literal replications and reproductions in OSF projects and keeps critical details in the main manuscript.
action: Create an OSF project documenting full procedural details of your literal replication.
quote: I share the extensive details of literal reproducibility and replication studies in Open Science Framework (OSF) projects

title: Compare your sample with the original
guidance: Present a table comparing your sample's demographics with the target study's before you report results, so reviewers understand sample differences first. When simple demographics are not enough, add tailored comparisons, such as a table of host countries across samples.
action: Build a table comparing your sample characteristics side by side with the original's.
quote: I recommend including a table of sample demographics that directly compares the sample in the current research to that of the target study.

title: Report results alongside the original's
guidance: Report your findings in the context of the target study, ideally in a table listing each hypothesis, whether it was supported in each study, and the corresponding statistics. Framing results as support for hypotheses keeps the focus on the phenomenon rather than on an adversarial comparison, while still clearly saying whether the original replicated.
action: Create a results table listing each hypothesis with support and statistics for original and replication.
quote: a table that lists hypotheses, whether each hypothesis was supported, and the corresponding statistical output

title: Don't overstate replication failure
guidance: It is tempting to overstate findings, for example by writing 'we failed to replicate Study X' when some ancillary findings did replicate. Be precise, and follow best practice in reporting boundary conditions and limitations; this builds confidence and makes the work read as less adversarial.
action: Check each conclusion sentence to ensure it matches exactly which findings did and didn't replicate.
quote: Researchers should be careful to be precise with language such that ﬁndings are not overstated.

title: Accept reasonable reviewer requests
guidance: Review teams often push replications to add theoretical contribution, such as extra studies or new variables, even when this departs from your purpose. Since outlets are limited, Obenauer recommends meeting ethical and reasonable requests to move the work toward publication.
action: When revising, accommodate ethical and reasonable reviewer requests that strengthen the contribution.
quote: As long as suggestions in the review process are ethical and reasonable, I encourage researchers to meet the requests of reviewers

title: Exact vs constructive replication
guidance: An exact replication tries to imitate its precedent study as closely as possible and can raise confidence or doubt about reported results. A constructive replication intentionally changes the population, data collection, analysis, or model to gather further evidence about the phenomenon.
action: Decide whether your study is an exact or a constructive replication and record why.
quote: An exact replication strives to imitate its precedent study very closely.

title: Replication needs new data; reproduction reuses data
guidance: Schwab et al. distinguish replications, which collect new data, from reproductions, which narrowly recreate the reported statistical results using the original authors' dataset. They also note that no replication can exactly repeat a prior study.
action: Confirm whether your project collects new data (replication) or reanalyses original data (reproduction).
quote: Replications require the collection of new data, whereas reproductions focus narrowly on the statistical recreation of the results reported in the precedent study

title: Options for a constructive replication
guidance: A constructive replication can change the studied population, the data collection, the analysis (e.g., Bayesian methods), or the model tested (e.g., adding or replacing a control variable), or use a more sophisticated measure. Choose the change that best serves your question.
action: Specify which single element (population, data collection, analysis, or model) your constructive replication changes.
quote: changing intentionally either the studied population, data collection, data analysis, or the model tested

title: Keep intentional changes focused and narrow
guidance: Every intentional change to the precedent design is a 'slippery slope' because it adds alternative explanations for any difference in results. To keep comparisons with the precedent study interpretable, keep deliberate changes highly focused and narrow.
action: Limit and list intentional design changes, and justify why each is needed.
quote: to facilitate comparisons with the precedent study, any intentional changes should be highly focused and narrow

title: Exact replications still have deviations
guidance: No replication repeats a prior study exactly; for a study to count as an exact replication, its deviations must be minor or irrelevant. Document every deviation and argue why it does or does not matter.
action: List every deviation from the precedent study and argue why each is minor or relevant.
quote: For exact replications, deviations must be considered minor or not relevant

title: Fill gaps in reported methods
guidance: Published studies never fully describe their decisions, and crucial but less obvious details are often missing, so replications face missing-information problems. Fill the gaps by learning standard practices, searching the literature, and consulting other researchers, possibly including the original authors.
action: List unreported design details and resolve each via literature, colleagues, or the original authors.
quote: To ﬁll these gaps, students must search the literature and consult fellow researchers, possibly including the authors of the precedent studies.

title: Expect missing information in the original
guidance: Studies cited by Schwab et al. could not reproduce about 70% of sampled published articles because crucial information was missing, and replications that need new data likely face even bigger gaps. Check how completely your target is reported before committing.
action: Audit the target paper for missing methodological information before committing to it.
quote: could not reproduce the results of about 70% of the published articles they sampled, because of crucial missing information.

title: Prefer targets with registered materials
guidance: Studies registered on platforms such as the Open Science Framework, or with online supplements, often provide sampling details, original data, code, and other information beyond the paper. This makes replication more feasible and higher quality.
action: Check whether candidate targets have OSF registrations, data, code, or supplements available.
quote: pointing students toward replicating studies that have been registered on platforms such as the Open Science Framework

title: Use the precedent's impact as a baseline
guidance: Old, rarely cited studies are unlikely to be fruitful targets, whereas highly cited, award-winning, or recent studies with rising citations signal topics of current interest. The precedent's contribution is a baseline for your replication's potential contribution.
action: Check the precedent's citations, awards, and citation trend when judging its potential contribution.
quote: replicating old studies with very few citations is unlikely to be very fruitful.

title: Estimate the value added of your replication
guidance: Doubts about reported findings can motivate a replication because a markedly different result would substantially correct existing knowledge. Fresh replications of already well-replicated studies add little, except well-designed constructive replications.
action: Check how often the target has been replicated and state what your replication would add.
quote: fresh replications of already well-replicated studies promise only rather minor additional contributions

title: Look for methodological and boundary-condition opportunities
guidance: When selecting a precedent, consider whether you can substantively improve its methods or probe key contingencies and boundary conditions. These opportunities strengthen the replication's contribution.
action: Note possible methodological improvements and boundary conditions you could test with each candidate.
quote: opportunities for substantive methodological improvements, and probing for key contingencies and boundary conditions are always important considerations

title: Expect and interpret differences carefully
guidance: Exact replication is extremely difficult and often impossible, so some differences between precedent and replication are to be expected. Asking only whether the replication 'confirms or rejects' the original misses its most important contributions; interpret differences with care.
action: Plan how you will interpret differences, beyond a binary replicated/not-replicated verdict.
quote: differences between precedents and replicates should be expected, and interpreted carefully

title: Focus on effect sizes and cumulative methods
guidance: Rather than binary significance-test verdicts, focus on effect sizes and the accuracy of their estimates, and consider Bayesian and/or meta-analytic techniques to compare and integrate precedent and replication findings.
action: Plan to compare effect sizes and intervals, and consider a meta-analytic or Bayesian comparison.
quote: replicators should focus more on effect sizes and the accuracy of effect size estimates, as well as consider applying Bayesian and/or meta-analytic techniques

title: Weigh design and context differences when interpreting
guidance: Interpretation needs more than choosing a statistical technique: consider how differences in measures, samples, research design, execution, and context could explain the results. This takes more work but gives deeper, theory-relevant insight.
action: For each result difference, list design, sample, measure, and context differences that might explain it.
quote: replicators need to also consider the impact of differences in measures, samples, and other research design, research execution, and research context factors

title: Adopt an accumulation-focused mindset
guidance: The aim of replication is to add evidence, not to overturn prior studies. Your central puzzle should be how the precedent and replication findings combine into a deeper understanding of the phenomenon and of how methods affect results.
action: Frame your discussion around what precedent and replication jointly show about the phenomenon.
quote: replicators’ central puzzle should be how to combine the ﬁndings of precedent studies and their replicates

title: Treat mismatches as clues
guidance: A mismatch between your results and the precedent's is a reason to search for explanations, which can reveal inherent uncertainties associated with specific effects. Such knowledge is valuable input for theory development and refinement.
action: Write down candidate explanations for any mismatch with the original findings.
quote: a mismatch between the ﬁndings of a replication and its precedent study is a good reason to search for possible explanations

title: Explain how the replication advances theory
guidance: Replications usually make incremental contributions whose value is subtle, so explain convincingly how your work advances theory. For instance, rather than just reporting that results differed in another country, interpret them as evidence about a theory's boundary conditions and practical implications.
action: Draft a paragraph interpreting your results in terms of theory and boundary conditions.
quote: describing the results in terms of evidence about a theory’s boundary conditions, and its attendant implications for practice

title: Link results back to your motivation
guidance: Close the loop in your paper: connect the replication results explicitly to the arguments in your introduction about why this precedent needed replicating.
action: Check that the discussion explicitly revisits each reason for replication given in the introduction.
quote: Aspiring authors should also carefully link the results of their replication back to the arguments in the introduction

title: Consider a series of related replications
guidance: Instead of a single replication, you might run a series, for example an exact replication combined with constructive replications that apply additional measures or analyses to the new data. Comparing constructive results with both the precedent and your exact replication enables finer-grained interpretation and can meet editors' expectations for strong evidence.
action: Consider pairing an exact replication with one or more constructive replications on the same data.
quote: Student teams, for example, can combine an exact replication with various types of constructive replications

title: Review the research leading to the precedent
guidance: A high-quality review of the research leading up to the precedent study can reveal dominant themes, trends, data biases, and overlooked causes, which a constructive replication might then address. It also helps you integrate your findings and highlight your contribution in the discussion.
action: Write a focused review of the research history leading up to your precedent study.
quote: One such strategy has been to provide high-quality reviews of the research leading up to precedent studies.

title: Frame findings to avoid defensiveness
guidance: Replication is contested territory, and editors are likely to invite the precedent's authors as reviewers. Because the studies usually provide complementary information rather than one being 'right', frame your findings to minimise defensive reactions.
action: Reread your abstract and discussion to remove wording that casts the original as 'wrong'.
quote: authors of replications should strive to frame their ﬁndings in ways that reduce the likelihood of defensive responses

title: Don't rule out top journals
guidance: Well-designed replications have appeared in top management journals, and suitably crafted replication manuscripts can still target the best outlets, especially if the precedent was published there. Table 2 of the article lists journals that have recently published replications.
action: Include in your list of target journals the journal that published the precedent study.
quote: suitably crafted manuscripts reporting replications can still beneﬁt from targeting what are considered to be the very best outlets

title: Combine replication with an extension
guidance: Framing replication and novel research as either/or misses synergies. A paper that reports both a replication-oriented and an extension-oriented study is, the authors argue, more likely to be published than either alone.
action: Consider adding an extension study so the paper reports both replication and extension.
quote: A resulting carefully crafted paper reporting both replication-oriented and extension-oriented empirical studies surely has a higher publication probability

title: Replications supplement, not replace, other training
guidance: Schwab et al. argue that replications add experiential learning alongside seminars and faculty-student research apprenticeships rather than replacing them. Design curricula so replication complements existing research training.
action: Position student replications as a complement to seminars and faculty research collaborations.
quote: replications should supplement and certainly not replace other types of research projects.

title: Use an early replication as a learning accelerator
guidance: Expecting first-year students to finish a top-journal novel project is ambitious; a first-year replication can build transferable skills that improve later original studies and make students more valuable contributors to faculty collaborations.
action: Consider assigning a replication as a first-year doctoral research project.
quote: conducting a replication during their ﬁrst year can serve as a learning accelerator

title: Align the target with student interests
guidance: Mentors should consider what students already know and discuss their research interests, so replication builds skills relevant to their future research. Incorporating students' own learning objectives into target choice increases motivation and can support the dissertation.
action: Discuss the student's learning objectives and research interests before choosing a precedent study.
quote: students are able to express their personal learning objectives and incorporate them when choosing a precedent study to replicate.

title: Steer students toward feasible targets
guidance: Because more than two-thirds of published studies may be hard to replicate owing to incomplete reporting, mentors, with their knowledge of the literature, should steer students away from studies with obvious replication obstacles and toward feasible ones.
action: Screen student-proposed targets for obvious feasibility problems before approving them.
quote: faculty mentors should guide their students away from studies that appear likely to pose obvious replication challenges

title: Match design changes to learning goals
guidance: Constructive replications offer flexibility: deliberate design changes can target each student's learning objectives, for example applying both frequentist and Bayesian analyses, or moving from observational to (quasi-)experimental designs. More experienced students can take on more challenging deviations.
action: Choose constructive design changes that match each student's methodological learning objectives.
quote: Intentional changes in the design of the replication study can address the speciﬁc learning objectives of each doctoral student.

title: Know when to intervene
guidance: Students learn more deeply when they find problems, weigh options, and try solutions themselves, which the precedent study's guidance makes possible. Mentors must judge when to step in and when to let students work on their own.
action: Agree on check-in points where the mentor reviews decisions, leaving room for independent problem solving.
quote: Successful mentors also have to make good decisions about when to intervene and when to let students proceed on their own.

title: Mentors safeguard replication quality
guidance: Replication projects often go wrong, so mentors are needed to ease frustration and suggest solutions. They should ensure the replication is well executed, uses appropriate methods, draws reasonable inferences, and presents arguments convincingly.
action: Review the student's methods, inferences, and arguments at key milestones.
quote: Mentors should ensure that replications are done well, that appropriate methodologies are being used, that inferences are reasonable

title: Let students replicate collaboratively
guidance: Students working together can debate how to implement the replication, what to infer, and how to write it up, with more experienced students helping less experienced ones. Students can also choose studies using methods they know, or ones that make them try newly learned methods.
action: Pair or group students so they can debate implementation, inference, and write-up decisions.
quote: Collaborating students can also debate with each other how to implement the replication, what inferences to draw

title: Share replication training resources
guidance: Platforms such as the Institute for Replication, OSF, the Center for Open Science, the Replication Wiki, Project TIER, and FORRT support reproduction and replication training. Table 1 of the article lists these and other resources for mentors to share.
action: Share a curated list of replication resources (e.g., OSF, I4R, Replication Wiki, FORRT) with students.
quote: Table 1 lists these and other emerging internet resources that faculty mentors can share with their students.

title: Coordinate multi-site student replications via CREP
guidance: The Collaborative Replication Education Project (CREP) on OSF coordinates independent student replications of highly cited, feasible studies, allowing their results to be published together meta-analytically. Such initiatives also teach abductive and inductive reasoning.
action: Check whether CREP offers a coordinated replication your students could join.
quote: provides a platform on which to coordinate multiple independent student replications of speciﬁc highly cited and feasible precedent studies

title: Replications teach what to report
guidance: Doing a replication shows students the full range of design decisions researchers make, including mundane tasks such as recruitment, coding, and ethics approval, and teaches them what information their own reports must include so others can replicate them.
action: Have students list which missing details hindered their replication and include them in their own reports.
quote: teaches students what information to include in their own future research reports to enable replications.
